0.title: Micah: What Does the LORD Require?
0.overview:
The message. Micah’s name means “Who is like the LORD?”, and his book ends by asking the same question in wonder: “Who is a God like you, pardoning iniquity and passing over transgression for the remnant of his inheritance?” (7:18). The holy God will not overlook a people who seize the poor man’s field, buy their judges and still say, “Is not the LORD in the midst of us?” (3:11); he comes down to judge, and even Jerusalem will fall. But judgment is not his last word. Out of the ruins he will gather a remnant, raise up a King from little Bethlehem to shepherd them, and “cast all our sins into the depths of the sea” (7:19). No one is like this God, so holy and so ready to forgive.

Background: the prophet. Micah came from Moresheth (1:1), called Moresheth-gath in 1:14, a farming town in the Shephelah, the low hills some twenty miles southwest of Jerusalem, near the Philistine border. A countryman, he sees the capital from the side of the small farmer whose land a powerful man wants: “They covet fields and seize them, and houses, and take them away” (2:2). Against paid prophets he claims only the power of “the Spirit of the LORD” (3:8).

When and where. He preached “in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah” (1:1), from about 740 to 700 BC, alongside Isaiah and Hosea, soon after Amos (see the kings of Israel and Judah). These were the years when Assyria swallowed the small nations of the west one by one. Ahaz bought Assyria’s help with the temple’s silver and gold, and even burned his son as an offering (2 Kings 16:3, 7–8); the worshipper of 6:7 who offers “my firstborn for my transgression” was no fantasy. Samaria, the northern capital, fell in 722 BC, as Micah had warned (1:6). In 701 BC Sennacherib took “all the fortified cities of Judah” (2 Kings 18:13), among them Lachish and the towns of Micah’s own district (1:10–16). Hezekiah turned to the LORD, and Jerusalem was spared (2 Kings 19:35–36).

A sermon remembered. A century later, about 609 BC, Jeremiah was on trial for his life for preaching that the temple would fall. Some of the elders defended him by quoting Micah: “Zion shall be plowed as a field; Jerusalem shall become a heap of ruins, and the mountain of the house a wooded height” (3:12; Jeremiah 26:18). Hezekiah had not put Micah to death, they said; he feared the LORD, and the LORD relented (Jeremiah 26:19). A warning had done its work.

The kind of writing. Micah is prophecy, almost all in Hebrew poetry. It speaks as a courtroom, with God as witness (1:2; 6:1–2); as a lament, with a pun on nearly every town’s name (1:10–16); and finally as prayer and hymn (7:14–20). Its promises reach beyond Micah’s day. Read with the New Testament, Zion lifted high and the nations streaming to learn God’s ways are fulfilled as Christ reigns and the gospel goes to the world, and will be completed in the new creation.

How the book makes its case. The book falls into three rounds, each opening with the call “Hear” (1:2; 3:1; 6:1), and each passing from judgment to hope. In the first (chapters 1–2) God comes down against both capitals and the land-grabbers; then, without warning, a gathered flock follows a King who breaks open the way: “Their king passes on before them, the LORD at their head” (2:13). In the second (chapters 3–5) rulers devour the flock, prophets preach for pay, and Zion is ploughed like a field; then the same hill is raised above every mountain, the nations come to be taught, and “they shall beat their swords into plowshares” (4:3). The road runs through Babylon, where God will redeem his people (4:10), to a ruler born in Bethlehem who “shall be their peace” (5:5). In the third (chapters 6–7) God takes his people to court and answers the frightened worshipper with 6:8; Micah finds “no one upright” (7:2), but he looks to the LORD and waits (7:7), and the book ends in praise of the God who pardons (7:18–20).

Did Micah write it all? Since the nineteenth century many scholars have held that only chapters 1–3, or most of them, come from Micah, and that the promises of chapters 4–7 were added after the exile, partly because 4:10 names Babylon as the place of exile more than a century early. But hope breaks into the judgment from the start (2:12–13); the promises answer the threats, the hill ploughed in 3:12 becoming the hill raised in 4:1; and Isaiah in the same years told Hezekiah that his treasures and sons would be carried to Babylon (Isaiah 39:6–7). This commentary’s view is that the book comes from Micah himself, gathered from his preaching over many years, and that the God who declares “the end from the beginning” (Isaiah 46:10) can name a city before its time.

Micah 6:8: a way to earn God’s favour? “He has told you, O man, what is good; and what does the LORD require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God?” (6:8) is often quoted as if it described a goodness that needs no Saviour. Micah rules that out. Before God asks anything, he recalls what he has already done: “For I brought you up from the land of Egypt and redeemed you from the house of slavery” (6:4). The verse shows how redeemed people live, not the price of redemption, and since no one lives it fully (7:2), it drives us to the One who did.

Where it leads: to Christ. Micah leads to Christ by promise, by the need it exposes, and by the God it reveals. The promise is plainest in 5:2: “But you, O Bethlehem Ephrathah, who are too little to be among the clans of Judah, from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel, whose coming forth is from of old, from ancient days.” When Herod asked where the Christ was to be born, the chief priests answered from this verse: “for from you shall come a ruler who will shepherd my people Israel” (Matthew 2:6). This commentary reads “from ancient days” as pointing beyond David’s ancient line to the eternal Son, born in David’s town. He is the shepherd Micah’s rulers never were: “he shall stand and shepherd his flock in the strength of the LORD” (5:4), and Jesus said, “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11). He does not merely bring peace: “he shall be their peace” (5:5), and Paul writes, “he himself is our peace” (Ephesians 2:14). Micah’s great question is answered at the cross, where God put forward his Son “as a propitiation by his blood” (Romans 3:25), so that he could pardon iniquity and remain just. Zechariah, John the Baptist’s father, sang that God was now keeping “the oath that he swore to our father Abraham” (Luke 1:73), the oath on which Micah ends (7:20).

For us. Micah asks whether our faith makes us honest at work, fair to the weak and humble before God, or whether, like Jerusalem’s leaders, we lean on the LORD while living as we please. He shows us how to wait for God in the dark: “But as for me, I will look to the LORD; I will wait for the God of my salvation; my God will hear me” (7:7). Above all he sends us to the God who “delights in steadfast love” (7:18). We do not do justice and love kindness to win his mercy; we learn to, because in Christ he has trodden our iniquities underfoot and cast all our sins into the sea.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — A Witness Against His People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Lord GOD himself comes to judge his people, and nothing can stand before him. The book opens as a courtroom: the peoples and the whole earth are summoned to hear, and God is the witness (vv. 1–2). Then the Judge steps out of his place, and the mountains melt and the valleys split beneath his feet (vv. 3–4). The charge is precise: the sin of the nation is centred in its capitals, Samaria in the north and Jerusalem in the south (v. 5). Samaria comes first. The proud city on its hill will be tipped into the valley until its foundations show, and the idols bought with the wages of unfaithfulness will be smashed and carried off (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology: God himself comes down to judge, and the sin of his people begins at the places they are proudest of.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD that came to Micah of Moresheth in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, which he saw concerning Samaria and Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word that follows is not Micah’s opinion but the LORD’s word, given to a countryman in a particular time and aimed at the two capitals.

Micah of Moresheth. Micah was a country man. Moresheth (called Moresheth-gath in v. 14) was a small farming town in the low hills southwest of Jerusalem, near the Philistine border, a long way from palace and temple.

In the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. Roughly the second half of the eighth century BC. That makes him a contemporary of Isaiah, who names the same kings (Isaiah 1:1), and of Hosea (Hosea 1:1), just after Amos.

Concerning Samaria and Jerusalem. The capitals of the northern and southern kingdoms. Samaria would fall to Assyria in 722 BC, within Micah’s lifetime, and Jerusalem would be surrounded in 701.

A sermon remembered. His words outlived him. A century later, when Jeremiah was on trial for his life for preaching against Jerusalem, the elders recalled that “Micah of Moresheth prophesied in the days of Hezekiah”, and that the king repented instead of putting him to death (Jeremiah 26:18–19). A country preacher’s sermon had changed a king’s heart.
verseByVerse.note: Micah prophesied about 740–700 BC. Moresheth is usually identified with Tel Judeideh, near Beth Guvrin, some 20 to 25 miles (35 km) southwest of Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear, you peoples, all of you; pay attention, O earth, and all that is in it, and let the Lord GOD be a witness against you, the Lord from his holy temple. For behold, the LORD is coming out of his place, and will come down and tread upon the high places of the earth. And the mountains will melt under him, and the valleys will split open, like wax before the fire, like waters poured down a steep place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole earth is summoned to watch as God himself comes down to judge, and creation itself cannot bear his coming.

Hear, you peoples, all of you. The book opens like a courtroom, with the peoples and the earth itself as the jury. (Where the ESV has “all of you”, its note says the Hebrew reads “all of them”.) The witness against the accused is the Lord GOD himself, speaking “from his holy temple”, his throne in heaven. When God is both witness and judge, the case is not in doubt.

The LORD is coming out of his place. Picture a king rising from his throne to deal with something himself. He will “tread upon the high places of the earth”, the hilltops and the hill shrines alike. And the world cannot bear it. Mountains melt “like wax before the fire”; valleys tear open; rock runs downhill like water. A psalm says the same: “The mountains melt like wax before the LORD” (Psalm 97:5).

Not small or safe. We speak easily of God’s love, and rightly, but the Bible will not let us make him small or safe. If mountains cannot stand before him, neither can we, except through the One who stood in our place. For God did come down again, not as Micah’s hearers expected but in Bethlehem, a few miles from Micah’s hills, and there the Judge took the judgment on himself.

verseByVerse.quote: All this is for the transgression of Jacob and for the sins of the house of Israel. What is the transgression of Jacob? Is it not Samaria? And what is the high place of Judah? Is it not Jerusalem? Therefore I will make Samaria a heap in the open country, a place for planting vineyards, and I will pour down her stones into the valley and uncover her foundations. All her carved images shall be beaten to pieces, all her wages shall be burned with fire, and all her idols I will lay waste, for from the fee of a prostitute she gathered them, and to the fee of a prostitute they shall return.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The judgment falls because of sin, and the sin is centred in the capitals, so Samaria, with all its idols, will be tipped into the valley.

For the transgression of Jacob. Why is God coming down? Not on a whim, but “for the transgression of Jacob”. Then Micah asks two questions and gives two shocking answers. Where is the transgression of the north? Samaria, the capital. Where is the “high place”, the shrine, of the south? Jerusalem, the city of the temple.

Corruption at the top. Sin was flowing downhill from the centres of power and worship. The places that should have led the nation to God were leading it away. When the church or its leaders go wrong, the damage runs through everything.

I will make Samaria a heap. Samaria, a walled city on a hill, will be tipped down the slope until its bare foundations show and farmers plant vines where the streets used to be. It happened in 722 BC, when “the king of Assyria captured Samaria, and he carried the Israelites away to Assyria” (2 Kings 17:6).

From the fee of a prostitute. The carved images and idols will be destroyed along with the city. The prophets use prostitution throughout for unfaithfulness to God, and here it may also be literal: prostitution was linked with the shrines of Canaan, and their treasuries may have been enriched by it. What was paid for with “the fee of a prostitute” will be lost the same shameful way, carried off as plunder. Whatever people build on idols returns to nothing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–16 — A Lament over the Towns
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prophet mourns as judgment rolls from Samaria to the gate of Jerusalem. He strips and howls like a jackal, because the incurable wound of the north has spread into Judah (vv. 8–9). Then he walks us through the towns of his own district, the low hills southwest of Jerusalem, and turns almost every town’s name into a pun on its fate as an invading army advances (vv. 10–15). Lachish, the great chariot city, is singled out as where Judah’s sin began, and Micah does not spare his own home town. The chapter ends with parents told to shave their heads in mourning for children going into exile (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: God's messenger weeps over the judgment he announces, and judgment reaches the ordinary villages, not only the capitals.

verseByVerse.quote: For this I will lament and wail; I will go stripped and naked; I will make lamentation like the jackals, and mourning like the ostriches. For her wound is incurable, and it has come to Judah; it has reached to the gate of my people, to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prophet does not announce judgment coolly but breaks down in grief, because the incurable wound has spread from Samaria to the gate of Jerusalem.

I will lament and wail. Micah goes “stripped and naked”, the dress of a prisoner of war or a mourner who has lost everything (see mourning customs). He howls like the desert animals, “like the jackals” and “the ostriches”, whose cries carry across the night.

Her wound is incurable. Samaria’s wound cannot be healed, and the infection is spreading south. It “has reached to the gate of my people, to Jerusalem”. That happened in 701 BC, when Sennacherib took Judah’s fortified cities and his officers stood outside Jerusalem’s walls (2 Kings 18:13, 17).

The Servant’s wounds. Samaria’s wound could not be healed. But Isaiah, preaching in the same years, saw a Servant whose own wounds would heal others: “he was pierced for our transgressions” and “with his wounds we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5). And Micah’s tears point ahead to a greater Prophet who came near Jerusalem, “saw the city, he wept over it” (Luke 19:41).

A true prophet’s grief. This is what distinguishes a true prophet from a bitter one. Micah says the hardest things in this book, and he weeps while he says them. Anyone who speaks God’s warnings without grief should ask whether he has understood them.

verseByVerse.quote: Tell it not in Gath; weep not at all; in Beth-le-aphrah roll yourselves in the dust. Pass on your way, inhabitants of Shaphir, in nakedness and shame; the inhabitants of Zaanan do not come out; the lamentation of Beth-ezel shall take away from you its standing place. For the inhabitants of Maroth wait anxiously for good, because disaster has come down from the LORD to the gate of Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Micah leads a funeral march through the towns of his own district, turning each town’s name into its sentence, and insists the disaster comes from the LORD.

A funeral march. The towns are villages of the Shephelah, where Micah grew up, along the line of an invading army toward Jerusalem.

Tell it not in Gath. A quotation. David said it when Saul and Jonathan died: “Tell it not in Gath, publish it not in the streets of Ashkelon” (2 Samuel 1:20), meaning, do not let the enemy hear of our disgrace.

Wordplay on the towns. In Hebrew nearly every line is a pun on a town’s name, which the English can only hint at. Beth-le-aphrah (“house of dust”) must roll in the dust; Shaphir (probably “beautiful”) goes out in shame; Zaanan (which sounds like “go out”) does not come out; Maroth (which sounds like “bitter”) waits in vain for good. Micah turns each town’s own name into its sentence.

Disaster has come down from the LORD. See where the trouble originates. Assyrian soldiers will do the damage, but Micah will not let his hearers treat it as bad luck or mere politics. The verb echoes verse 3: the LORD came down, and so disaster comes down.

Uncertain wording. This is some of the hardest Hebrew in the prophets. Several towns cannot now be located, and some puns rest on likely rather than certain meanings of the names. The Beth-ezel line (v. 11) is especially obscure; it seems to mean that Beth-ezel, itself in mourning, can give its neighbours no support. The overall sense is clear.
verseByVerse.note: All these towns lay in the Shephelah, within a day or two's walk of Moresheth. Several, such as Shaphir, Zaanan and Beth-ezel, cannot now be located with certainty.

verseByVerse.quote: Harness the steeds to the chariots, inhabitants of Lachish; it was the beginning of sin to the daughter of Zion, for in you were found the transgressions of Israel. Therefore you shall give parting gifts to Moresheth-gath; the houses of Achzib shall be a deceitful thing to the kings of Israel. I will again bring a conqueror to you, inhabitants of Mareshah; the glory of Israel shall come to Adullam. Make yourselves bald and cut off your hair, for the children of your delight; make yourselves as bald as the eagle, for they shall go from you into exile.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fortress of Lachish, where Judah’s trust in military strength began, will flee, Micah’s own town will be handed over, and parents will mourn children going into exile.

Harness the steeds to the chariots. Lachish was the second city of Judah, a great fortress guarding the road to Jerusalem, and a chariot base. Its name sounds like the Hebrew for “steeds” (rekesh), so the chariot city is told to harness its horses, but for flight.

The beginning of sin to the daughter of Zion. The “daughter of Zion” is Jerusalem. Lachish is probably called the beginning of her sin because this was where Judah put its trust in horses and military strength instead of God, and where the idolatry of the north came south. In 701 BC Lachish became the Assyrian army’s headquarters (2 Kings 18:14, 17), and its fall was carved in stone on the walls of Sennacherib’s palace.

Parting gifts to Moresheth-gath. Now Micah names his own home town. The “parting gifts” (the ESV notes this may mean a dowry) were what a father gave a daughter when she left home for good, and Moresheth sounds like a word for “betrothed”. Micah’s village is being handed over like a bride to a foreign power. He does not exempt his own people from the message. The wordplay runs on: Achzib sounds like akzab, “a deceitful thing”, and Mareshah probably like the word for “conqueror”.

The glory of Israel shall come to Adullam. Adullam was the cave country where David hid from Saul (1 Samuel 22:1). The “glory of Israel”, the nation’s leaders and wealth, will end up hiding there as fugitives, as David did before he became king.

Make yourselves bald. Shaving the head was a public sign of grief (Isaiah 22:12). The chapter ends with parents told to mourn as at a funeral, because “the children of your delight” are going into exile. Sin is never private: the next generation pays for it.

Warnings that need not come true. Yet remember what Jeremiah’s generation remembered about Micah (v. 1): a king listened and repented, and God relented. Warnings like this are given by a merciful God so that they need not come true.

Uncertain wording. Micah does not say why Lachish was “the beginning of sin”; the link with chariots and military trust fits best but is an inference. “Parting gifts” and some of the puns are also uncertain. The direction is plain: the towns guarding Jerusalem fall one by one.
verseByVerse.note: Sennacherib's carved reliefs of the siege of Lachish, from his palace at Nineveh, are now in the British Museum.

1.title: The LORD Comes Down
1.overview:
Where we are. This is the opening of the book, and the first of its three rounds, each beginning with the call “Hear” (see the introduction). Before Micah names a single sin, he shows us who is coming: the Lord himself, stepping out of his heavenly temple to judge.

The message. The holy God is coming down to deal with his people’s sin, and nothing can stand before him: mountains melt like wax. The rot is worst where privilege is greatest, in the two capitals, Samaria and Jerusalem, so judgment will begin with them and roll through the towns until it reaches the gate of Jerusalem. Yet the prophet who announces it weeps, for God takes no pleasure in the ruin he must bring.

Why it was said. Israel and Judah were prosperous and religious, and their capitals felt safe. Assyria was already swallowing the nations of the west; Samaria would fall in 722 BC and Sennacherib’s army would sweep through Micah’s own district in 701 BC (see the introduction). Micah tells them why it is happening and who is behind it.

How the chapter makes its case. The courtroom is opened, with the earth as jury and God as witness (v. 2). The Judge comes down, and creation gives way beneath his feet (vv. 3–4). The charge follows: the sin of the nation is centred in its capitals (v. 5), so Samaria will be tipped into the valley and its idols smashed (vv. 6–7). Then the tone changes. The prophet strips and howls, because the incurable wound has reached Jerusalem’s gate (vv. 8–9), and he walks us through a dozen towns of his own district, turning each name into a pun on its fate, as the invader advances toward the capital (vv. 10–16).

Where it leads. Chiefly by the character of God revealed in Christ, and by the need the chapter exposes. The God who comes down in judgment here came down in a manger, “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), and the judgment that melts mountains fell on him at the cross, so that those who trust him can stand in the presence of a holy God. And the weeping prophet is a faint outline of the Saviour who saw Jerusalem and “wept over it” (Luke 19:41), before going out to bear its judgment himself.

For us. Do not make God small or safe; the One we pray to makes mountains run like wax, and only Christ makes it safe to draw near. Take sin seriously, especially where you have influence, because it never stays private. And if you must speak hard truths to others, speak them as Micah did, with tears.
1.theology:
God summons the whole earth as witness and comes down himself to judge; no created thing can stand before him (vv. 2-4; Ps 97:5).

Sin is most serious where privilege is greatest, and corruption at the centres of power and worship spreads through a whole nation (v. 5).

What is built on idols and gained by filth returns to nothing (vv. 6-7).

God's messenger weeps over the judgment he must announce (v. 8).

Human wounds may be incurable, but Christ's wounds heal (v. 9; Isa 53:5).

God rules the disasters that human armies inflict; they are never mere politics (v. 12).

Trust in military strength is itself a sin, and it spreads (v. 13).

Sin costs the next generation, and warnings are given so that they need not be fulfilled (v. 16; Jer 26:18-19).
1.examples:
God sent a country preacher from a farming town to accuse two capitals, and the first thing he shows them is mountains running downhill like wax before a fire. The God we pray to is not small or safe, and only the One who stood in our place lets us stand before him.

Micah howls like a jackal over the message he has to deliver, then leads a funeral march through the villages where he grew up, ending with parents shaving their heads for children who will not come back. Hard truths are best spoken by people who grieve over them, and the sins of one generation are paid for by the next.

keyVerse.quote: For behold, the LORD is coming out of his place, and will come down and tread upon the high places of the earth.
keyVerse.note: Everything in the chapter follows from this: God himself is coming, and nothing, from mountains to fortified cities, can stand before him. It confronts every attempt to make God small or safe. And it prepares us for the wonder of the gospel, in which the same God came down not to tread on us but to be trodden on for us.

1.reflection:
Micah begins not with sin but with God coming down, and the mountains melting before him (vv. 3–4). Why does it matter that we see who God is before we hear what we have done wrong? How does Christ make it possible to stand before such a God?

The sin of the nation was centred in its capitals, the places of power and worship (v. 5). Where do you have influence, at home, at work or in church, and how might your choices there spread to others, for good or ill?

Micah weeps and howls over the judgment he announces (vv. 8–9). What would change in how we speak about sin, in our families or in public, if we spoke with Micah’s tears? Where do we see the same grief in Jesus?

The chapter ends with children going into exile because of their parents’ sin (v. 16). How does knowing that sin is never private help us resist it, and what hope does the gospel give those who are suffering for others’ sins?

Their king passes on before them, the LORD at their head.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Woe to Those Who Covet Fields
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Those who use their power to seize their neighbours’ inheritance will lose their own. Micah opens with a woe on men who lie awake plotting and rise at dawn to take fields and houses, simply because they can (vv. 1–2). Their sin is more than theft: each family’s field was its God-given share in the promised land. So God answers their plotting with his own. He devises disaster they cannot shake off, like a yoke on the neck (v. 3); they will sing a funeral song over their own lost fields as a foreign conqueror divides them (v. 4); and when the land is shared out again, they will have no one to measure a portion for them in the assembly of the LORD (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: God answers those who plot against their neighbours by plotting against them.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to those who devise wickedness and work evil on their beds! When the morning dawns, they perform it, because it is in the power of their hand. They covet fields and seize them, and houses, and take them away; they oppress a man and his house, a man and his inheritance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God pronounces woe on the powerful who lie awake planning to take what belongs to others and rise at dawn to do it, simply because they can.

Work evil on their beds. Micah takes us into the bedrooms of the powerful. They lie awake, not tossing with guilt but planning: how to get that piece of land, how to structure the loan so the farmer cannot repay. At first light they do it. And the reason is chillingly simple: “because it is in the power of their hand”. They can, so they do.

They covet fields and seize them. Follow the chain: covet, seize, take. The tenth commandment forbids the first step precisely because it leads to the others: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house” (Exodus 20:17).

A man and his inheritance. To an Israelite this was worse than theft. God had said, “The land shall not be sold in perpetuity, for the land is mine” (Leviticus 25:23), and each family’s field was its God-given inheritance, its share in the promise (see the Year of Jubilee). To take a man’s field was to cut him and his children out of what God had given them. Ahab did it to Naboth, who told him, “The LORD forbid that I should give you the inheritance of my fathers” (1 Kings 21:3). Isaiah, preaching at the same time as Micah, cried, “Woe to those who join house to house, who add field to field” (Isaiah 5:8).

A definition of wickedness. That is one of the plainest definitions of wickedness in the Bible: not “Is this right?” but “Can I get away with it?” Sin does not begin with what we finally do; it starts in what we rehearse in our minds. The cure is more than willpower. We need minds made new by the Spirit through God’s word, and a Saviour whose pure heart God counts as ours, because our own imaginations are not pure.

In our day. This still speaks wherever the strong use law, debt or paperwork to take from the weak what keeps them alive.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the LORD: behold, against this family I am devising disaster, from which you cannot remove your necks, and you shall not walk haughtily, for it will be a time of disaster. In that day they shall take up a taunt song against you and moan bitterly, and say, "We are utterly ruined; he changes the portion of my people; how he removes it from me! To an apostate he allots our fields." Therefore you will have none to cast the line by lot in the assembly of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers their plotting with his own: the men who seized other people’s fields will lose their own and have no share left among the LORD’s people.

I am devising disaster. They devised wickedness on their beds; now God says, “I am devising disaster.” The word for “disaster” is the same Hebrew word as the evil they planned (ESV note). God answers their plotting with plotting of his own. It will sit on “this family” like a yoke an ox cannot shake off. They have walked “haughtily” through the village, and they will not do it again.

To an apostate he allots our fields. The men who took other people’s fields will one day sing a funeral song about their own: a foreign conqueror will carve up their land. What we take unjustly, we do not keep.

None to cast the line by lot. When Israel entered the land, each family’s portion was measured out by lot before the LORD (Joshua 18:10). These men will have no one left to hold the measuring line for them; they have lost their place in “the assembly of the LORD” itself. Grabbing more and more of God’s gifts, they end with no share at all in the Giver.

The inheritance no one can seize. Jesus warned that “one’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions” (Luke 12:15), and those who trust him receive an inheritance no creditor or conqueror can touch.

Uncertain wording. Verse 4 is compressed Hebrew, and “apostate” is uncertain: it may mean a faithless one, a rebel, or the foreign captor. Either way, the fields pass to strangers.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: People who rob the weak silence God’s preachers, yet God will still gather and lead his flock. The people tell Micah to stop preaching, sure that disgrace cannot touch them (v. 6). God answers that his words do good to the upright (v. 7), while his own people behave like an enemy army, stripping travellers and driving widows and children from their homes (vv. 8–9). The land is no longer a place of rest (v. 10), and the preacher they want would promise them wine and strong drink (v. 11). Then hope breaks in: God will gather the remnant like sheep in a fold, and their King, the LORD himself, will break through the gate and go before them (vv. 12–13).
verseByVerse.theology: People who silence God's word still have a future only because God keeps a remnant and goes before them himself.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not preach"—thus they preach— "one should not preach of such things; disgrace will not overtake us." Should this be said, O house of Jacob? Has the LORD grown impatient? Are these his deeds? Do not my words do good to him who walks uprightly?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people try to silence God’s preachers, but God replies that his words are harsh only to those who walk crookedly.

Do not preach. The people answer back, almost comically. They have their own sermon, and its text is that nobody should preach like this. Their confidence rests on a slogan: “disgrace will not overtake us.”

The same refrain in every age. Every generation says, “Say what you like about sin in general, but do not name ours.” Amos heard it at Bethel (Amos 7:12–13); and Paul warned of people who “will not endure sound teaching” (2 Timothy 4:3).

Has the LORD grown impatient? God answers with questions. (The ESV notes the Hebrew reads “Has the spirit of the LORD grown short?”) They are blaming the message on a bad mood in heaven, as though God had simply lost his temper. Judgment is not what God delights in; their own deeds have brought it.

Do not my words do good to him who walks uprightly? God’s word is not harsh; it feels harsh to people living crookedly. The same sunlight that comforts healthy eyes hurts inflamed ones. If Scripture seems to us only negative and restrictive, the problem may not be with Scripture.

verseByVerse.quote: But lately my people have risen up as an enemy; you strip the rich robe from those who pass by trustingly with no thought of war. The women of my people you drive out from their delightful houses; from their young children you take away my splendor forever. Arise and go, for this is no place to rest, because of uncleanness that destroys with a grievous destruction. If a man should go about and utter wind and lies, saying, "I will preach to you of wine and strong drink," he would be the preacher for this people!
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s own people have become an enemy army, preying on travellers, widows and children, and they want a preacher who promises good times.

My people have risen up as an enemy. They rob travellers who “pass by trustingly”, stripping the rich robe from people who expect no danger.

The women of my people. The victims are widows and children. Women are evicted from “their delightful houses”, the homes their husbands left them, and the children lose “my splendor”, the dignity and inheritance God himself had given them. Note that word “my”. God calls their inheritance his own splendour. Rob a child of his future, and you are robbing God.

This is no place to rest. The promised land was meant to be Israel’s place of rest. Now God says “this is no place to rest.” A society that devours its weakest has made its own home uninhabitable, and exile is coming. The rest the land pointed to is found in Christ (Matthew 11:28).

I will preach to you of wine and strong drink. Send them a preacher who talks of plenty and good times, and they will pack the building. “Wind and lies” is what they want. Preaching that only ever promises prosperity and never mentions sin is not new, and it is not kindness; it leaves people comfortable on the way to ruin.

The god who never says no. Every age wants a preacher made in its own image. Micah’s hearers wanted prosperity; ours, on the whole, want affirmation. The god many people believe in today is pleasant and undemanding: he wants us happy and feeling good about ourselves, helps when asked, and otherwise keeps out of the way. It is hard to imagine anyone fearing him, or being changed by him. But such a god never names our sin, and so he can never forgive it; he never says no, and so his yes means nothing. A love that approves of everything has stopped paying attention. The God of Micah tells the truth about the stolen fields because he cares about the widows, and even about the thieves. And in Christ he went further than any prophet: he told us the worst about ourselves and then bore it himself. Only a God who says no to our sin can say a yes to us worth having, “for all the promises of God find their Yes in him” (2 Corinthians 1:20).

Uncertain wording. Verses 8–9 are difficult Hebrew. The ESV notes that “pass by trustingly” may mean “returning from war”, and “my splendor” could be the children’s inheritance, dignity or place among God’s people. The charge is plain: the strong prey on the defenceless.

verseByVerse.quote: I will surely assemble all of you, O Jacob; I will gather the remnant of Israel; I will set them together like sheep in a fold, like a flock in its pasture, a noisy multitude of men. He who opens the breach goes up before them; they break through and pass the gate, going out by it. Their king passes on before them, the LORD at their head.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Without warning God promises to gather the remnant of his people like a flock, and their King, the LORD himself, will break through and lead them out.

I will gather the remnant of Israel. Micah turns like this all through his book, because judgment is never God’s last word for his people. The word “remnant” matters: God does not promise to save everyone in that generation, but he will always have a people of his own, gathered “like sheep in a fold” (see shepherds and sheepfolds). Some readers take these verses as more judgment, a flock penned up ready to be driven away. But the words fit a rescue better: a pasture, a noisy multitude, a king going before them.

He who opens the breach goes up before them. Picture a flock penned in a walled town. Someone smashes an opening in the wall, and the sheep pour out after him into the open country.

Their king passes on before them. Who is he? Micah gives two names in one line: “Their king” and “the LORD at their head”. The king who breaks the wall is God himself. Later the book will say where that king is born (5:2).

Someone goes first and makes an opening. Christians cannot read this without thinking of Jesus. He is the shepherd who “calls his own sheep by name and leads them out”, and “goes before them” (John 10:3–4). He broke open the way through death itself, going ahead “as a forerunner on our behalf” (Hebrews 6:20). Every believer trapped by sin, guilt or fear should hear this verse: there is someone who goes first and makes an opening.

2.title: The Breaker Goes Up Before Them
2.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 showed God coming down to judge Samaria and Jerusalem. Chapter 2 names the sin that brings him, closes the first round of the book, and ends it, as every round ends, with hope (see the introduction).

The message. God sees the powerful lying awake to plan how to take what belongs to the weak, and he is planning too: those who grab other people’s inheritance will lose their own. People who rob the helpless do not want a preacher who names it; they want one who promises good times. But God’s last word is not judgment. He will gather a remnant like a flock, and their King, the LORD himself, will break open the way and go before them.

Why it was said. In Micah’s Judah, wealthy men were using debt, courts and plain force to swallow the family fields of small farmers, the land God had given each household as its inheritance (see the introduction). And they had preachers who assured them that disgrace would never overtake them.

How the chapter makes its case. A woe falls on men who plot at night and seize fields at dawn because they can (vv. 1–2). God answers plot with plot: they will wear a yoke they cannot shake off, mourn their own lost fields and have no share left in the assembly of the LORD (vv. 3–5). The people answer back, “Do not preach” (v. 6), and God replies that his words do good to the upright (v. 7), while they strip travellers and evict widows and children (vv. 8–10), and would gladly hire a preacher of wine and strong drink (v. 11). Then, without warning, comes the promise: God will gather his flock, and their King will break through the gate before them (vv. 12–13).

Where it leads. By promise. The King who goes before his flock and breaks open the way is “the LORD at their head” (v. 13), and the New Testament finds him in Jesus, the good shepherd who “goes before” his sheep and leads them out (John 10:4), and who has broken through death itself as our forerunner. He is also the true inheritance the land-grabbers forfeited: in him the poor in spirit receive a share that no one can seize.

For us. Watch what you rehearse on your bed at night, and never use power simply because you can. Welcome preaching that names your sin, because only a God who tells you the truth can forgive you. And if you feel hemmed in by guilt, fear or your own history, remember that someone has gone ahead and made an opening.
2.theology:
Sin begins in the imagination, and the powerful without conscience do wrong simply because they can (v. 1).

Property taken from the weak is taken from God, who gave each family its inheritance (vv. 2, 9; Lev 25:23; 1 Kgs 21:3).

God repays scheming with judgment that fits the crime, and what is grabbed unjustly is not kept (vv. 3-5).

God's word does good to the upright; it is only bitter to those who are living crookedly (v. 7).

People get the preachers they want, and comfortable preaching is not kindness (vv. 6, 11; 2 Tim 4:3).

God always preserves a remnant, and judgment is never his last word for his people (v. 12).

God himself goes before his people to break open a way out, fulfilled in Christ the shepherd-king and forerunner (v. 13; John 10:3-4; Heb 6:20).
2.examples:
Men lie awake planning how to take a neighbour's field and carry it out at first light because nobody can stop them; in the end they sing a funeral song over their own lost fields. Wherever the strong use debt or paperwork to take from the weak what keeps them alive, this chapter still speaks.

The people’s favourite sermon is “Do not preach”, and the preacher they want talks of wine and good times while widows are put out of their homes. Against all that, Micah sets a wall broken open and a flock pouring out after its king, the Christ who goes ahead of his people and makes a way out.

keyVerse.quote: He who opens the breach goes up before them; they break through and pass the gate, going out by it. Their king passes on before them, the LORD at their head.
keyVerse.note: After a chapter of greed, eviction and false preaching, this verse is God’s last word: a King who breaks open the way for his trapped flock and goes first. Micah names him as both king and LORD, and the New Testament shows him to us in Jesus, the shepherd who leads his sheep out and the forerunner who has gone through death ahead of us.

2.reflection:
The powerful plan evil on their beds and do it at dawn “because it is in the power of their hand” (v. 1). Where are we tempted to do something simply because we can? What do we rehearse in our minds at night?

The people said, “Do not preach” about such things (v. 6), and wanted a preacher of “wine and strong drink” (v. 11). What kinds of preaching do people in our culture want to hear, and why is a God who never says no unable to save?

God calls the children’s inheritance “my splendor” (v. 9). Who are the defenceless in our community, and what would it look like to protect what God has given them?

The chapter ends with a King who breaks open the way and goes before his flock (vv. 12–13). Where do you feel hemmed in, and how does Jesus as the one who goes first give you hope?

Is it not for you to know justice?—<sup>2</sup>you who hate the good and love the evil, who tear the skin from off my people and their flesh from off their bones,<sup>3</sup>who eat the flesh of my people, and flay their skin from off them, and break their bones in pieces and chop them up like meat in a pot, like flesh in a cauldron.<sup>4</sup>Then they will cry to the LORD, but he will not answer them; he will hide his face from them at that time, because they have made their deeds evil.<sup>5</sup>Thus says the LORD concerning the prophets who lead my people astray, who cry "Peace" when they have something to eat, but declare war against him who puts nothing into their mouths.<sup>6</sup>Therefore it shall be night to you, without vision, and darkness to you, without divination. The sun shall go down on the prophets, and the day shall be black over them;<sup>7</sup>the seers shall be disgraced, and the diviners put to shame; they shall all cover their lips, for there is no answer from God.<sup>8</sup>But as for me, I am filled with power, with the Spirit of the LORD, and with justice and might, to declare to Jacob his transgression and to Israel his sin.<sup>9</sup>Hear this, you heads of the house of Jacob and rulers of the house of Israel, who detest justice and make crooked all that is straight,<sup>10</sup>who build Zion with blood and Jerusalem with iniquity.<sup>11</sup>Its heads give judgment for a bribe; its priests teach for a price; its prophets practice divination for money; yet they lean on the LORD and say, "Is not the LORD in the midst of us? No disaster shall come upon us."<sup>12</sup>Therefore because of you Zion shall be plowed as a field; Jerusalem shall become a heap of ruins, and the mountain of the house a wooded height.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Rulers Who Hate the Good
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Leaders whose whole task is justice have become butchers of the people they were meant to protect, and God will not answer their prayers. Micah calls the heads of Jacob to hear, and asks the question that convicts them: is it not your job to know justice? (v. 1). Instead they hate good and love evil, and he describes what they do to the people in the language of a slaughterhouse: skinning, breaking bones, chopping up meat for the pot (vv. 2–3). The picture shows how God sees land-grabbing, rigged courts and unpaid wages. So when trouble comes and they cry to the LORD, he will hide his face from them (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: Leaders exist to know and do justice, and God will not hear those who have devoured the people he gave them.

verseByVerse.quote: And I said: Hear, you heads of Jacob and rulers of the house of Israel! Is it not for you to know justice?— you who hate the good and love the evil, who tear the skin from off my people and their flesh from off their bones, who eat the flesh of my people, and flay their skin from off them, and break their bones in pieces and chop them up like meat in a pot, like flesh in a cauldron. Then they will cry to the LORD, but he will not answer them; he will hide his face from them at that time, because they have made their deeds evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rulers whose task is justice have turned on the people they were meant to protect, and when they cry to God he will not answer them.

Is it not for you to know justice? Micah turns to the men who sat in the courts and ran the country. His question is almost gentle, and it cuts deep: justice is the one thing they exist for. Instead they “hate the good and love the evil”. Then comes language of shocking violence: the rulers are butchers, skinning people, breaking their bones, chopping them up “like meat in a pot”.

A picture, not a report. This is a picture, not a report of cannibalism. But it is a picture God chose. What these men actually did was take land, charge ruinous interest, fix court cases and keep back wages. In heaven’s view, that is butchery. Remember that when injustice is discussed in the polite language of policy and markets: God describes it in the language of a slaughterhouse.

The true shepherd. These leaders fed on the flock; Jesus gave himself for it: “the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45).

He will not answer them. The day will come when these same men pray, and God will not answer. Isaiah told the same generation, “even though you make many prayers, I will not listen; your hands are full of blood” (Isaiah 1:15). There is a kind of prayer God refuses, not because he cannot hear, but because the one praying has no intention of changing. God’s mercy is open to everyone who turns from sin, but it is not a way to escape the consequences while keeping the sin.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Religious leaders who sell God’s word will lose it, and a city built on corruption will be ploughed under. The prophets cry “Peace” to whoever feeds them, so night will fall on their visions and God will give them no answer (vv. 5–7). Micah, by contrast, is filled with the Spirit of the LORD to tell Israel its sin (v. 8). Then he gathers the whole leadership together: rulers who twist justice and build Zion with blood, judges, priests and prophets who all work for a price, yet who lean on the LORD and feel safe (vv. 9–11). Because of them Zion will be ploughed as a field (v. 12), a warning that once brought a king to repentance.
verseByVerse.theology: Ministry sold for money ends in silence from God, and religious confidence without obedience cannot save a city.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD concerning the prophets who lead my people astray, who cry "Peace" when they have something to eat, but declare war against him who puts nothing into their mouths. Therefore it shall be night to you, without vision, and darkness to you, without divination. The sun shall go down on the prophets, and the day shall be black over them; the seers shall be disgraced, and the diviners put to shame; they shall all cover their lips, for there is no answer from God. But as for me, I am filled with power, with the Spirit of the LORD, and with justice and might, to declare to Jacob his transgression and to Israel his sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Prophets who sell their message will be left in darkness, while Micah, filled with the Spirit, tells the truth about sin.

The prophets who lead my people astray. Feed them, and they cry “Peace”; give them nothing, and they declare war on you. They have turned the word of God into a product, and whoever pays decides what it says.

A word for paid ministry. That is a searching word for anyone in paid ministry today. It does not condemn supporting ministers; Scripture commands it. It condemns letting money shape the message: the sermon softened because a major giver is in the building, the sin never named because it is the sin of the people who pay the bills. Peter tells elders to serve “not for shameful gain, but eagerly” (1 Peter 5:2), and Paul says, “we are not, like so many, peddlers of God’s word” (2 Corinthians 2:17).

It shall be night to you. The punishment fits exactly. They sold visions, so the visions stop, and the sun goes down on men whose trade was light. They “cover their lips” in shame, because “there is no answer from God”. There are few more frightening judgments on a religious establishment than silence from God.

But as for me, I am filled with power. One man stands against the whole professional class, claiming nothing for himself. He is filled “with the Spirit of the LORD”, the only qualification that matters, and a gift. See what the Spirit produces in him: “justice and might”, and the courage “to declare to Jacob his transgression”. The Spirit does not make him popular; he makes him truthful. The greater Prophet would one day stand in a synagogue and say, “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me” (Luke 4:18), and speak the truth at the cost of his life.

Uncertain wording. In verse 5, “when they have something to eat” is literally “who bite with their teeth”. Most take it, as the ESV does, to mean prophets who preach peace while they are being fed; a few hear the bite of a snake. Either way, the fee decides the message.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear this, you heads of the house of Jacob and rulers of the house of Israel, who detest justice and make crooked all that is straight, who build Zion with blood and Jerusalem with iniquity. Its heads give judgment for a bribe; its priests teach for a price; its prophets practice divination for money; yet they lean on the LORD and say, "Is not the LORD in the midst of us? No disaster shall come upon us." Therefore because of you Zion shall be plowed as a field; Jerusalem shall become a heap of ruins, and the mountain of the house a wooded height.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because the whole leadership sells justice and religion while feeling safe in God, Zion itself will be ploughed like a field.

Who build Zion with blood. They “make crooked all that is straight”, bending a clear law until it serves them. The city was being beautified, and every fine new building was paid for by somebody’s ruin. God looks at the architecture and sees the blood in the mortar.

Its heads give judgment for a bribe. Here is the whole leadership of the nation in one verse: judges, priests and prophets, and all three have a price. Then the astonishing last line. These same men “lean on the LORD” and say, “Is not the LORD in the midst of us?” They were not atheists; they were orthodox. They had the temple, the sacrifices and the promises to David, and they treated all of it as insurance. Jeremiah met the same slogan a century later: “Do not trust in these deceptive words: ‘This is the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD’” (Jeremiah 7:4).

The test of confidence. The test of our confidence in God is what it produces. If it makes us humble, honest and generous, it is faith; if it lets us go on cheating people while feeling safe, it is superstition. Real faith rests not on our record but on Christ’s. He alone did justice perfectly, and his righteousness is counted to all who trust him. And the Spirit who filled Micah (v. 8) now lives in believers, so that their faith shows itself in honest lives. Where we have failed, the way back is confession and the mercy God promised (1 John 1:9), not a better slogan.

Zion shall be plowed as a field. A shocking thing to say in Jerusalem: farmers ploughing where Zion stood, the temple hill gone to scrub, and all “because of you”.

What became of the warning. Two things happened to this sentence. First, people listened. A hundred years later, when Jeremiah was on trial for saying something similar, the elders quoted this very verse and recalled that Hezekiah feared the LORD and sought his favour, so that God relented and Jerusalem was spared in Micah’s day (Jeremiah 26:18–19). One sermon, received in repentance, gave the city more than another hundred years. Second, when the warning was finally ignored, it came true: in 586 BC the Babylonians burned the temple and left the city in ruins. God’s patience is long, but it is not endless.

A greater temple. Jesus foretold the temple’s fall again (Mark 13:2), but offered one no army can plough: “the temple of his body” (John 2:21), raised on the third day.
verseByVerse.note: Hezekiah reigned about 715–686 BC; Jeremiah's trial came early in Jehoiakim's reign, about 609 BC (Jer 26:1), so Micah's words had been remembered for about a century.

3.title: Zion Shall Be Plowed as a Field
3.overview:
Where we are. The second round of the book opens with a fresh call to “Hear” (v. 1; see the introduction). Chapter 2 exposed the land-grabbers; now Micah turns to the people at the top, the rulers, priests and prophets of Jerusalem, and this round, like the first, will pass from judgment to hope in chapters 4 and 5.

The message. Those who lead God’s people will answer to God for how they use them. Rulers who should know justice are devouring the flock; prophets shape their message to the fee; and all of them lean on the LORD and feel safe. God will not answer such people, his word will fall silent among them, and the city they built with blood will be ploughed like a field. Against them stands one man with nothing to offer but the Spirit of the LORD and the courage to tell the truth.

Why it was said. Jerusalem was being enlarged and beautified, while its courts sold verdicts and its religious leaders sold guidance. They trusted the temple and God’s promises to David to keep them safe whatever they did (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. First the rulers: their task is justice, but they hate good, love evil and treat the people like meat for the pot, so when they cry to the LORD he will not answer (vv. 1–4). Then the prophets: they cry “Peace” to those who feed them and war on those who do not, so night will fall on their visions and God will give them no answer (vv. 5–7). In contrast stands Micah, filled with the Spirit to declare Israel’s sin (v. 8). Finally the whole leadership is summoned together: judges, priests and prophets all have their price, yet they say, “Is not the LORD in the midst of us?” (vv. 9–11). Therefore Zion will be ploughed as a field (v. 12).

Where it leads. By the need it exposes, and by pattern. Micah shows rulers, priests and prophets all failing at once, and the gospel shows one man who is all three and fails at none: the King who rules for his people’s good, the Priest who does not sell the way to God but gives himself, and the Prophet anointed with the Spirit (Luke 4:18) who would not trim his message to save his life. He too warned that the temple would be thrown down (Mark 13:2), and he offered his own body as the true temple, destroyed and raised in three days (John 2:19–21).

For us. Leadership in home, church, business or nation is a trust from God, and he judges those who use people instead of serving them. Do not let money or approval shape what you say is true. And test your confidence in God by what it produces: faith in Christ makes people humble and just; religion used as insurance lets them go on cheating while feeling safe.
3.theology:
Authority exists to know and do justice, and God holds leaders accountable for the people entrusted to them (v. 1).

Economic oppression is violence in God's eyes, however respectable its language (vv. 2-3).

Prayer offered without any intention of repenting will not be answered (v. 4; Isa 1:15).

Ministry shaped by money corrupts the message, and God answers it with silence (vv. 5-7; 2 Cor 2:17; 1 Pet 5:2).

The Spirit of the LORD makes his servants truthful rather than popular, and Christ is the supreme example (v. 8; Luke 4:18).

Religious confidence that does not change conduct is superstition, not faith (v. 11; Jer 7:4).

God’s warnings are meant to be heeded: when people repent, God relents, and when they ignore him, the warning comes true (v. 12; Jer 26:18-19).
3.examples:
Micah describes judges whose one job is justice and who hate it, and he calls their oppression not policy but a slaughterhouse. Their prayers go unanswered, because they mean to change nothing; God’s mercy is wide open, but not to those who mean to keep their sin.

A prophet whose message depends on who bought his dinner ends up covering his mouth because heaven has gone quiet. A city with blood in the mortar of its fine buildings will see a ploughman working where the temple stood. Yet the same warning, heard humbly, spared Jerusalem for a century.

keyVerse.quote: But as for me, I am filled with power, with the Spirit of the LORD, and with justice and might, to declare to Jacob his transgression and to Israel his sin.
keyVerse.note: In a chapter of leaders who sell justice and prophets who sell visions, this verse stands alone: one man whose only qualification is the Spirit of the LORD, and who uses it to tell the truth. It shows what true ministry is, and it points to Jesus, anointed with the same Spirit, who spoke the truth at the cost of his life.

3.reflection:
Micah describes unjust rulers as butchers (vv. 2–3). Why do you think God chose such violent language for things like rigged courts and unpaid wages? How does it change the way we think about injustice described in polite terms?

The prophets cried “Peace” when they were fed, and changed their message when they were not (v. 5). In what ways can money, approval or fear shape what we say is true, in church, at work or among friends?

Micah’s only strength was the Spirit of the LORD (v. 8). What does the Spirit produce in Micah, and what does that teach us about courage and faithfulness today?

Jerusalem’s leaders sold justice yet said, “Is not the LORD in the midst of us?” (v. 11). How can we tell the difference between real faith in God and religion used as insurance? How does Christ, the true temple, change where we look for God’s presence?
