verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The Mountain of the House of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s purpose for Zion does not end in ruins: in the latter days the nations will come to be taught by him, and his rule will bring a peace no treaty can. The hill that was to be ploughed (3:12) is lifted above every mountain, and the peoples flow to it (v. 1). They come asking to be taught God’s ways, and his word goes out from Jerusalem (v. 2). As judge of the nations he settles their disputes, so swords become ploughshares and war is forgotten (v. 3), and everyone sits unafraid under his own vine and fig tree (v. 4). Meanwhile, though the nations follow other gods, God’s people resolve to walk in his name for ever (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: God's future is a world of nations taught by him and at peace, and it begins wherever people come to learn his ways.

verseByVerse.quote: It shall come to pass in the latter days that the mountain of the house of the LORD shall be established as the highest of the mountains, and it shall be lifted up above the hills; and peoples shall flow to it, and many nations shall come, and say: "Come, let us go up to the mountain of the LORD, to the house of the God of Jacob, that he may teach us his ways and that we may walk in his paths." For out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem. He shall judge between many peoples, and shall decide disputes for strong nations far away; and they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks; nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war anymore;
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the latter days God’s house will be honoured above every place on earth, the nations will come to be taught his ways, and his rule will bring such peace that weapons become farm tools.

In the latter days. The final era of God’s dealings with the world, which the New Testament says began with the coming of Christ. Zion was in fact a modest ridge, lower than the hills around it. The height is not physical but a matter of honour: God’s house will be honoured above every place on earth.

Peoples shall flow to it. See the direction of travel. Rivers run downhill, but here the peoples flow up to the mountain. Micah pictures the impossible: the nations of the world streaming uphill to the God of Israel.

Come, let us go up to the mountain of the LORD. Nobody drives them; they invite each other. And what they want is not spectacle or political favours but teaching, “that he may teach us his ways and that we may walk in his paths.” They learn in order to obey.

Out of Zion shall go forth the law. The traffic then reverses. The nations come to Zion, and from Zion “the word of the LORD” goes out to the nations (the ESV notes that “law” may be rendered “teaching”).

They shall beat their swords into plowshares. When God is the judge everyone accepts, weapons become useless. A sword is hammered into a ploughshare that opens the ground for seed; a spear becomes a pruning hook for the vines. The metal is not thrown away; it is repurposed for life. And the very knowledge of war is lost: “neither shall they learn war anymore.”

Micah and Isaiah. These three verses are almost word for word the same as Isaiah 2:2–4. Micah and Isaiah preached in the same years in the same city; perhaps one quoted the other, or both drew on a message already known. Either way, God said it twice.

Beginning from Jerusalem. This is what began at Pentecost. The risen Christ said that repentance and forgiveness “should be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24:47), and the word has been going out from Zion ever since. Christ did not win this peace with a sword but through the cross, “thereby killing the hostility” (Ephesians 2:16). Until the promise is complete, the church lives it in advance: every time enemies are reconciled in Christ, a sword becomes a plough.

Is this a call to disarmament now? It promises the peace God will bring when he judges the nations; Joel even turns the picture round for the day of battle: “Beat your plowshares into swords” (Joel 3:10). Christians seek peace (Romans 12:18), but the state still “does not bear the sword in vain” (Romans 13:4); the full peace comes with Christ’s reign.

Doesn’t religion cause most wars? The objection has real history behind it: crusades, wars of religion, terror in the name of God. But the record is more tangled than the slogan. Most wars have been fought over land, power and nation, and the twentieth century, the bloodiest yet, saw its worst killing done by regimes that had openly thrown God out. The trouble is not religion as such but the human heart, which will fight for whatever it worships, whether a god, a race, a class or a flag. Micah does not offer less worship as the cure for war. He offers truer worship. The nations stop learning war when they are taught by the LORD and accept him as judge, because only a judge everyone trusts can end the cycle of grievance.

Where Christians differ. Christians understand the timing of this promise differently. Many in the Reformed tradition see it being fulfilled now, in part, as people from every nation come to Christ, are taught his ways and are reconciled to one another in his church. Many premillennial and dispensational Christians expect a literal future age in which Christ reigns from Jerusalem and the nations come there. All agree that the promise is completed only when Christ returns, when “the nations” will walk by the light of the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:24). Faithful Christians hold each of these views.

This commentary’s view. This commentary takes the first view, because it fits the New Testament better, which tells believers, “you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God” (Hebrews 12:22), and sees the nations coming in through the gospel (Acts 15:14–17). The promise is fulfilled in Christ’s present reign and the spread of the gospel, and completed in the new creation.
verseByVerse.note: Micah alone adds the vine and fig tree of verse 4; Isaiah's version of the oracle (Isa 2:2–4) has nothing corresponding to it.

verseByVerse.quote: but they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree, and no one shall make them afraid, for the mouth of the LORD of hosts has spoken. For all the peoples walk each in the name of its god, but we will walk in the name of the LORD our God forever and ever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s peace means everyone safe and unafraid in his own home, guaranteed by God’s own word, and in the meantime his people walk in his name though the nations do not.

Under his vine and under his fig tree. This is what peace looks like in the Bible, and it is beautifully ordinary: a person sitting outside his own house, under his own vine and fig tree, with nothing to fear. In Solomon’s best days Israel had briefly known it: “every man under his vine and under his fig tree” (1 Kings 4:25).

No one shall make them afraid. Chapter 2 described men whose fields and houses were stolen. Here everyone has his own place, and keeps it. And the guarantee is not a treaty: “the mouth of the LORD of hosts has spoken.”

We will walk in the name of the LORD our God. Now the response of faith in the meantime. The world is full of other gods, and God’s people are a minority. Very well: we will walk in his name: not someday, when the nations come, but now, while they have not yet come.

The believer’s stance. This is the believer’s stance in every generation. We do not wait for the culture to change before we live for God. We walk in the name of the LORD our God, who has already made us his own, and by his Spirit we walk in it “forever and ever.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–13 — The Lame Shall Be the Remnant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The road to that glorious future runs through weakness and exile, and God is in control all the way. He will gather the lame and the cast off and make them a strong nation over which he reigns, and the former kingship will return to Zion (vv. 6–8). But first Zion must writhe like a woman in labour, leave the city and go to Babylon, and there the LORD will rescue her (vv. 9–10). Many nations gather to gloat over her, not knowing that God has gathered them like sheaves to the threshing floor; Zion will thresh them, and their wealth will be devoted to the Lord of the whole earth (vv. 11–13).
verseByVerse.theology: God builds his kingdom out of the broken and the exiled, and the enemies who think they have gathered against him have been gathered by him.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day, declares the LORD, I will assemble the lame and gather those who have been driven away and those whom I have afflicted; and the lame I will make the remnant, and those who were cast off, a strong nation; and the LORD will reign over them in Mount Zion from this time forth and forevermore. And you, O tower of the flock, hill of the daughter of Zion, to you shall it come, the former dominion shall come, kingship for the daughter of Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will build his kingdom out of the lame, the scattered and the afflicted, reign over them for ever, and restore the kingship to Zion.

I will assemble the lame. Who will make up this glorious kingdom? God lists them: the lame, the driven away, the cast off, and, most startling of all, “those whom I have afflicted”. He does not pretend the affliction came from somewhere else. These are the stragglers of the flock, the ones who cannot keep up. He builds his kingdom out of the people the world discards. Paul would say it plainly: “God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong” (1 Corinthians 1:27).

The lame I will make the remnant. If you feel like one of the lame, this verse is for you. It does not say, “God will heal you and then use you”; it says, “the lame I will make the remnant.” And this is exactly the company Jesus gathered: “the blind receive their sight and the lame walk” (Matthew 11:5), and his parable’s banquet is filled with “the poor and crippled and blind and lame” (Luke 14:21).

O tower of the flock. A tower of the flock was a watchtower in the fields where a shepherd kept watch over the sheep (see shepherds and sheepfolds). Jerusalem is addressed as that tower. What is certain is the promise: “the former dominion”, the kingship of David’s line, is coming back. Micah’s next chapter will name the village it comes from (5:2).

Uncertain wording. “Tower of the flock” is Migdal-eder, and Genesis mentions a “tower of Eder” near Bethlehem (Genesis 35:21); some connect the two, though we cannot be sure. “Hill” is ophel, probably Jerusalem’s fortified mound by the palace.

verseByVerse.quote: Now why do you cry aloud? Is there no king in you? Has your counselor perished, that pain seized you like a woman in labor? Writhe and groan, O daughter of Zion, like a woman in labor, for now you shall go out from the city and dwell in the open country; you shall go to Babylon. There you shall be rescued; there the LORD will redeem you from the hand of your enemies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zion’s present agony is like labour pain, leading to birth, not death: she must go into exile in Babylon, and there the LORD will rescue her.

Like a woman in labor. From the glorious future Micah turns abruptly to the painful present: the city screams, and her king and counsellor are useless. Labour pain is agony, but it is not the pain of dying; it is the pain of something being born. God’s judgments on his people are never merely destructive. Jesus used the same picture for his disciples’ grief before Easter (John 16:21).

You shall go to Babylon. Micah is preaching in the eighth century BC, when Assyria is the world power and Babylon, ancient and famous though it is, is a subject city. Yet he names Babylon as the place of exile, more than a century before it happened. Some scholars conclude the line must have been added later; the church has generally taken it as it stands, for a God who declares “the end from the beginning” (Isaiah 46:10) can name a city. Isaiah, in the same years, warned Hezekiah that his treasures and descendants would be carried to Babylon (Isaiah 39:6–7), so Micah does not stand alone (see the introduction).

There you shall be rescued. The rescue happens there: not before the exile, not instead of it, but in it. God does not usually spare his people the fire of trouble; he meets them in it. Many a Christian has found that the place they begged to be delivered from was the place God came to them.

verseByVerse.quote: Now many nations are assembled against you, saying, "Let her be defiled, and let our eyes gaze upon Zion." But they do not know the thoughts of the LORD; they do not understand his plan, that he has gathered them as sheaves to the threshing floor. Arise and thresh, O daughter of Zion, for I will make your horn iron, and I will make your hoofs bronze; you shall beat in pieces many peoples; and shall devote their gain to the LORD, their wealth to the Lord of the whole earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The nations gather to gloat over Zion, but God has gathered them like sheaves for threshing, and he will give his weak people the victory and himself the spoil.

Let our eyes gaze upon Zion. The enemies gather, and their motive is ugly: they want to see Zion humiliated, to gaze at her shame. There is a cruelty in the human heart that enjoys watching the fall of something beautiful.

He has gathered them as sheaves to the threshing floor. One of the great sentences of the Bible for God’s people under pressure. The nations think they have assembled themselves; in fact God has gathered them, like sheaves brought to the threshing floor. They are not the harvesters; they are the harvest. They do not know God’s thoughts or understand his plan. Neither, often, do we. The comfort is not that we can see the plan, but that there is one.

Arise and thresh, O daughter of Zion. Threshing was done by driving oxen over the grain. God turns his limping, exiled people into the ox on the threshing floor, with a horn of iron and hoofs of bronze.

Devote their gain to the LORD. The point of the victory is not plunder. The spoil is to be devoted to the LORD (the ESV notes the Hebrew is “devote to destruction”, the word for what is handed over wholly to God), because he is “the Lord of the whole earth”. Every victory God gives belongs to him.

The plan they did not know. The supreme case came at the cross: rulers gathered against God’s anointed, sure they had won, yet Jesus was “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God” (Acts 2:23), and their apparent victory became his. Since Christ came, the church’s weapons are not iron, for “we do not wrestle against flesh and blood” (Ephesians 6:12). But the shape of the promise holds: the people who look defeated are the ones God will use, and the outcome belongs to him.

4.title: Swords into Plowshares
4.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 3 ended with the temple hill ploughed like a field. Chapter 4 begins on the same hill and sees it lifted above every mountain: the second round of the book (chapters 3–5) passing, like the first, from judgment to hope (see the introduction).

The message. The ruin of Zion is not the end of God’s purpose. In the latter days his house will be honoured above every place on earth, the nations will come to be taught his ways, and his rule will bring a peace so complete that weapons become farm tools and everyone sits unafraid under his own vine. The way there runs through weakness and exile: God will build his kingdom from the lame and the cast off, rescue his people in Babylon, and turn the enemies gathered against them into a harvest.

Why it was said. Micah’s hearers had just been told that Jerusalem would become a heap of ruins (3:12), and Assyria was crushing the nations around them (see the introduction). They needed to know whether God’s promises to Zion and to David had died with their leaders’ sins.

How the chapter makes its case. First the far horizon: the mountain of the LORD raised high, the nations streaming to it to learn, the LORD judging between them, and swords beaten into ploughshares (vv. 1–4). In the meantime God’s people resolve to walk in his name (v. 5). Then three “now” scenes, each turning from distress to hope. God will gather the lame and make them a strong nation, and the former kingship will return to Zion (vv. 6–8). Zion writhes like a woman in labour, goes to Babylon, and is rescued there (vv. 9–10). The nations gather to gloat, not knowing that God has gathered them like sheaves for threshing (vv. 11–13).

Where it leads. By promise. The risen Jesus said that repentance and forgiveness “should be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24:47): from Pentecost onward the word of the LORD has gone out from Zion, and people of every nation have come to be taught by him. He is the King whose “former dominion” returns, born in the village Micah names next (5:2); he gathered the lame and the outcast (Matthew 11:5); and he makes peace by the cross, not the sword (Ephesians 2:14–16). What has begun now will be completed when he returns.

For us. Do not wait for the world to change before you walk in the name of the LORD; walk in it now. If you feel lame, driven away or cast off, you are exactly the kind of person God builds his kingdom from. And when enemies seem to gather, remember that they do not know God’s plan, and that every time enemies are reconciled in Christ a sword becomes a plough.
4.theology:
God's final purpose is not a ruined hill but a world of nations coming to be taught by him (vv. 1-2; Isa 2:2-4).

Real peace comes from submitting disputes to God's judgment, and it turns weapons into tools (v. 3).

The peace God promises is ordinary and secure: every family safe in its own place (v. 4; 1 Kgs 4:25).

Believers walk in God's name now, without waiting for the nations to join them (v. 5).

God builds his kingdom out of the lame, the cast off and the afflicted (vv. 6-7; 1 Cor 1:27).

God's rescue often comes in the place of exile rather than instead of it (v. 10).

Enemies who assemble against God's people have in fact been gathered by God, whose plan they do not know (vv. 11-13).
4.examples:
A ploughed-over temple hill is lifted above every mountain, and the nations invite each other uphill to be taught. A sword is beaten flat into a blade that opens the soil for seed, and a man sits under his own fig tree with nothing to fear. Every time enemies are reconciled in Christ, that promise is lived in advance.

The limping stragglers of the flock become a strong nation, and the armies who think they are the harvesters turn out to be the harvest. If you feel like one of the stragglers, God has not left you behind; he builds his kingdom from people like you.

keyVerse.quote: and many nations shall come, and say: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the LORD, to the house of the God of Jacob, that he may teach us his ways and that we may walk in his paths.” For out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem.
keyVerse.note: This is the heart of the chapter’s hope: the nations coming not for plunder or politics but to be taught by God and to obey him. It is being fulfilled as the gospel goes out from Jerusalem to the world, and it explains why swords become ploughshares in the next verse: only when people learn God’s ways does war end.

4.reflection:
Micah pictures the nations streaming uphill to be taught God’s ways (vv. 1–2). Where do you see this happening in the world today? What does it mean for us that people come “that we may walk in his paths,” and not only to learn?

Swords become ploughshares when God judges between the nations (v. 3). Where in your relationships is there a “sword” that needs to become a plough, and how does the cross make that possible?

God builds his kingdom from the lame, the driven away and the afflicted (vv. 6–7). How does this encourage you when you feel weak? How should it shape who our church welcomes?

Zion is rescued in Babylon, not before it (v. 10), and her enemies do not know God’s plan (v. 12). How have you experienced God meeting you in trouble rather than sparing you from it?

5.text: <sup>1</sup>Now muster your troops, O daughter of troops; siege is laid against us; with a rod they strike the judge of Israel on the cheek.<sup>2</sup>But you, O Bethlehem Ephrathah, who are too little to be among the clans of Judah, from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel, whose coming forth is from of old, from ancient days.<sup>3</sup>Therefore he shall give them up until the time when she who is in labor has given birth; then the rest of his brothers shall return to the people of Israel.<sup>4</sup>And he shall stand and shepherd his flock in the strength of the LORD, in the majesty of the name of the LORD his God. And they shall dwell secure, for now he shall be great to the ends of the earth.<sup>5</sup>And he shall be their peace. When the Assyrian comes into our land and treads in our palaces, then we will raise against him seven shepherds and eight princes of men;<sup>6</sup>they shall shepherd the land of Assyria with the sword, and the land of Nimrod at its entrances; and he shall deliver us from the Assyrian when he comes into our land and treads within our border.<sup>7</sup>Then the remnant of Jacob shall be in the midst of many peoples like dew from the LORD, like showers on the grass, which delay not for a man nor wait for the children of man.<sup>8</sup>And the remnant of Jacob shall be among the nations, in the midst of many peoples, like a lion among the beasts of the forest, like a young lion among the flocks of sheep, which, when it goes through, treads down and tears in pieces, and there is none to deliver.<sup>9</sup>Your hand shall be lifted up over your adversaries, and all your enemies shall be cut off.<sup>10</sup>And in that day, declares the LORD, I will cut off your horses from among you and will destroy your chariots;<sup>11</sup>and I will cut off the cities of your land and throw down all your strongholds;<sup>12</sup>and I will cut off sorceries from your hand, and you shall have no more tellers of fortunes;<sup>13</sup>and I will cut off your carved images and your pillars from among you, and you shall bow down no more to the work of your hands;<sup>14</sup>and I will root out your Asherah images from among you and destroy your cities.<sup>15</sup>And in anger and wrath I will execute vengeance on the nations that did not obey.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers a besieged and humiliated people with a King born in a small village. Jerusalem is surrounded and its ruler is struck on the cheek (v. 1), but God turns to Bethlehem, too little to count among the clans of Judah, and promises a ruler whose coming forth is from ancient days (v. 2). His people must wait until a promised birth; then the scattered brothers return, and he shepherds them in the LORD’s strength, great to the ends of the earth (vv. 3–4). He will be their peace, and when the Assyrian invades, God will raise more than enough shepherds and the King will deliver his people (vv. 5–6).
verseByVerse.theology: God's answer to a besieged world is a ruler born in a village, whose origins are ancient and whose reign reaches the ends of the earth.

verseByVerse.quote: Now muster your troops, O daughter of troops; siege is laid against us; with a rod they strike the judge of Israel on the cheek. But you, O Bethlehem Ephrathah, who are too little to be among the clans of Judah, from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel, whose coming forth is from of old, from ancient days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jerusalem is besieged and its king humiliated, God promises a ruler of his own choosing from little Bethlehem, whose coming forth is from ancient days.

With a rod they strike the judge of Israel on the cheek. (In the Hebrew Bible this verse is numbered 4:14, as the ESV notes.) The city, “daughter of troops”, is under siege, and its king, the “judge of Israel”, is struck on the cheek with a rod, the way a slave might be hit. David’s throne has come to this.

But you, O Bethlehem Ephrathah. Verse 2 is the great word of the book. Against the humiliation of verse 1 God sets not Jerusalem but a farming village a few miles south, David’s home town, so small it was “too little to be among the clans of Judah”. God’s habit is to start in places nobody is watching.

For me. This king is God’s own choice, for God’s own purposes, as David was (1 Samuel 16:1).

From of old, from ancient days. A birth in a village is set beside a “coming forth” from ancient days. Many in the church, including the Reformed tradition, read this of the eternal origin of the Son of God, who was “in the beginning” with God (John 1:1) and “is before all things” (Colossians 1:17). Others take it of a family line reaching back to David and beyond. The first reading fits the language best: the child who would be born in Bethlehem was older than Bethlehem.

Bethlehem in the Gospels. Seven hundred years later, when Herod asked where the Christ was to be born, the chief priests answered at once: “In Bethlehem of Judea, for so it is written by the prophet” (Matthew 2:5). Their quotation calls Bethlehem “by no means least” (Matthew 2:6): the village was small, and God’s choice made it great.

The struck judge. Christians remember another judge of Israel struck on the face: “Then they spit in his face and struck him” (Matthew 26:67), as Isaiah had foreseen: “I gave my back to those who strike” (Isaiah 50:6). The King from Bethlehem bore the shame of David’s throne for his people.

The chief priests’ tragedy. They knew the verse, quoted it accurately, and stayed in Jerusalem while the foreigners went on to Bethlehem. Knowing the Bible is not the same as going to Christ.

How Jewish readers take it. Jewish tradition reads this verse of the Messiah, as the Targum and the chief priests of Matthew 2 did, but most Jewish interpreters understand “from of old” as descent from David’s ancient house, not existence before birth. On Bethlehem and the King from David’s line, Jewish and Christian readings agree. This commentary takes the further step, reading the ancient days as pointing to the Son who “was in the beginning with God” (John 1:2) and was born in Bethlehem (Luke 2:4–7).

Uncertain wording. In verse 1 the verb rendered “muster your troops” can also mean “gash yourself”, as mourners did (the same verb is used in 1 Kings 18:28), so some read it as the city slashing itself in grief; either way she is in distress. In verse 2 the Hebrew words behind “from of old, from ancient days” can mean ancient times or the days of eternity, which is why the King James Version has “from everlasting”; both point beyond an ordinary king.
verseByVerse.note: Verse 2 is 5:1 in the Hebrew Bible. Ephrathah was the old name of Bethlehem's district (Gen 35:19; Ruth 1:2), and it marks this Bethlehem off from another in Zebulun (Josh 19:15).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore he shall give them up until the time when she who is in labor has given birth; then the rest of his brothers shall return to the people of Israel. And he shall stand and shepherd his flock in the strength of the LORD, in the majesty of the name of the LORD his God. And they shall dwell secure, for now he shall be great to the ends of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After a time of suffering ended by a promised birth, the King will gather his scattered brothers and shepherd them in the LORD’s strength to the ends of the earth.

He shall give them up. Between promise and fulfilment lies a long wait: the exile, and centuries when no son of David reigned. The waiting is measured by a birth, “until the time when she who is in labor has given birth”. Isaiah, preaching alongside Micah, had spoken of a virgin who would “conceive and bear a son” (Isaiah 7:14).

The rest of his brothers shall return. The scattered people are gathered around the newborn King, and they are “his brothers”: he is one of them.

He shall stand and shepherd his flock. Micah has described leaders who fleeced and devoured the flock (3:1–3); here at last is a shepherd who feeds it, “in the strength of the LORD”, not his own, so that his people “dwell secure”.

The good shepherd. Jesus said, “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11), and he sent his people to all nations (Matthew 28:19). For a church that feels small and exposed, security rests not on its numbers but on the one who holds the staff.

Who is “she who is in labor”? Many read her as the mother of the Messiah, fulfilled in Mary; others as Zion herself, whose labour pains Micah has just described (4:9–10). The two belong together: Zion’s long labour ends when Mary’s Son is born. Until then God gives his people up to suffering; then the King comes and his brothers return.

verseByVerse.quote: And he shall be their peace. When the Assyrian comes into our land and treads in our palaces, then we will raise against him seven shepherds and eight princes of men; they shall shepherd the land of Assyria with the sword, and the land of Nimrod at its entrances; and he shall deliver us from the Assyrian when he comes into our land and treads within our border.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The coming King will himself be his people’s peace and will deliver them from every invading enemy.

He shall be their peace. Micah does not say “he shall bring peace” but “he shall be their peace”. Peace is not a policy he arranges; it is a person his people have. Paul writes of Christ, “he himself is our peace” (Ephesians 2:14).

Seven shepherds and eight princes of men. “The Assyrian” was the terror of Micah’s own day, and stands here for every hostile power that tramples God’s people. Against such an enemy God raises “seven shepherds and eight princes of men”. Hebrew often counts like this, naming a number and then one more, as Amos did: “For three transgressions of Damascus, and for four” (Amos 1:3). The sense is: more than enough. God is never short of deliverers.

The land of Nimrod. Another name for the region of Assyria and Babylon, going back to the mighty hunter whose kingdom began at Babel (Genesis 10:8–10). There is grim irony in the wording: the invaders came to shepherd others with the sword, and now they will be shepherded that way themselves.

He shall deliver us. The promise ends where it must. The rescue comes from the ruler himself, not from the seven shepherds.

What it does not mean. Shepherding Assyria with the sword first meant Judah’s deliverance from its great enemy. Its fulfilment is Christ’s victory over every hostile power, by the gospel now and at his return; it is no call to military conquest.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew behind “at its entrances” is unusual; with a slight change of vowels it reads “with the drawn sword”, matching the line before. The sense is the same either way.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–15 — Dew, Lion, and the End of False Trusts
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Under the coming King, God’s people become a blessing and a power among the nations, and God removes everything they trusted instead of him. Scattered among many peoples, the remnant will be like dew from the LORD, a gift no one can arrange, and like a lion no enemy can resist (vv. 7–9). Then, in a surprising turn, God cuts off Judah’s own horses, chariots, cities and strongholds, its sorceries and fortune-tellers, its carved images, pillars and Asherah poles (vv. 10–14). Stripped of false securities, they are left with him. The nations that will not obey face his wrath (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: God removes his people's false securities, not to leave them defenceless, but to leave them with himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the remnant of Jacob shall be in the midst of many peoples like dew from the LORD, like showers on the grass, which delay not for a man nor wait for the children of man. And the remnant of Jacob shall be among the nations, in the midst of many peoples, like a lion among the beasts of the forest, like a young lion among the flocks of sheep, which, when it goes through, treads down and tears in pieces, and there is none to deliver. Your hand shall be lifted up over your adversaries, and all your enemies shall be cut off.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Among the nations God’s people will be both a blessing from him alone, like dew, and a power no enemy can withstand, like a lion.

Like dew from the LORD. In Israel’s rainless summers the night dew kept crops alive, and no one arranges it: it does not “wait for the children of man”. So God’s scattered people are a quiet, God-given blessing wherever they are.

Like a lion among the beasts of the forest. The same people are dew to some and a lion to others. The hard image belongs to God’s judgment on nations that set themselves against him.

The gospel’s double effect. The New Testament says something similar about the gospel: to some it is the fragrance of life, and to others the smell of death (2 Corinthians 2:15–16). The church’s calling is to be dew; but the word we carry is not neutral, and those who refuse it are not left untouched.

The Lion who is a Lamb. The remnant’s strength is borrowed from its King, “the Lion of the tribe of Judah”, who conquered as “a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain” (Revelation 5:5–6), and his people overcome the same way: by the gospel and faithful suffering, not by the sword.

All your enemies shall be cut off. For a small, bullied people this was a promise to hold on to; for the church under pressure it still is.

verseByVerse.quote: And in that day, declares the LORD, I will cut off your horses from among you and will destroy your chariots; and I will cut off the cities of your land and throw down all your strongholds; and I will cut off sorceries from your hand, and you shall have no more tellers of fortunes; and I will cut off your carved images and your pillars from among you, and you shall bow down no more to the work of your hands; and I will root out your Asherah images from among you and destroy your cities. And in anger and wrath I will execute vengeance on the nations that did not obey.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will cut away everything his people trusted instead of him, weapons, fortresses, magic and idols, so that they lean on him alone; and he will judge the nations that refuse to obey.

I will cut off your horses. God has just promised victory, and now he destroys his own people’s equipment, again and again. First the military: horses, chariots and strongholds were what Judah had been trusting instead of God, as Micah has already said of Lachish (1:13). While they have a chariot corps they will trust it (compare Psalm 20:7).

I will cut off sorceries from your hand. Next the occult and the idolatrous. Sorcery and fortune-telling tried to control the future without God; carved images, sacred stone pillars and Asherah poles (wooden poles honouring the goddess Asherah) were the furniture of Canaanite worship, which Israel had mixed with the worship of the LORD.

The work of your hands. The phrase says what every idol is, ancient or modern: something we make, and then serve.

On the nations that did not obey. The chapter closes with the other side of the same coin. God purifies his people and judges the nations that will not listen. Both come from the same holiness, and both are settled by the ruler from Bethlehem, who is at once the shepherd of his flock and the judge of the earth.

Discipline as grace. God is not stripping his people bare out of spite. He is removing the things that would fail them, so that they are left holding on to the only One who will not: “For the Lord disciplines the one he loves” (Hebrews 12:6). Anyone who has watched God dismantle a quiet substitute for himself will recognise this list.

Horses and horoscopes. Horses and sorceries look like an odd pair, but they shared one purpose: both promised control. The chariot made you safe against the enemy you could see; the fortune-teller made you safe against the future you could not. Our versions are more respectable: the pension forecast, the security system, the watch that tracks our sleep. None of these is wrong. But we are tempted to believe that with enough planning nothing should surprise us, and when something does, we feel outrage as well as grief, as though a contract had been broken. The idol of control promises peace and produces anxiety, because there is always one more thing to manage. God does not make us careless; he takes the idol away and gives himself. The one in charge is the ruler from Bethlehem, who held all things and yet let himself be struck and crucified for us (compare v. 1). If he holds the future, we can plan with open hands, and sleep.

5.title: The Ruler from Bethlehem
5.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 5 completes the second round of Micah’s preaching (chapters 3 to 5). Chapter 4 lifted Zion above the mountains, then plunged her into labour pains and exile; now Jerusalem is surrounded and its king is struck in the face.

The message. When his people’s king is humiliated and the city besieged, God answers with a birth. Out of little Bethlehem he will raise a ruler whose coming forth is from ancient days, who will shepherd his flock in the LORD’s strength and will himself be their peace. And because that King is enough, God will strip from his people everything else they have trusted: horses, fortresses, fortune-tellers and idols.

Why it was said. Micah’s hearers lived in the shadow of Assyria, the superpower that swallowed Samaria and overran Judah’s towns, and their kings leaned on chariots, alliances and foreign gods (see the introduction). David’s line looked weak and shamed; the chapter promises that its true King will come from where the line began.

How the chapter makes its case. The besieged city and its struck judge (v. 1) are answered by the promise of a ruler from Bethlehem, “from ancient days” (v. 2). There will be a wait until a birth; then the scattered brothers return, and the King shepherds them, great to the ends of the earth (vv. 3–4). He is their peace, and against “the Assyrian”, the enemy of every age, God gives more than enough defenders (vv. 5–6). The remnant becomes dew among the nations and a lion against its enemies (vv. 7–9). Last, God cuts away horses, cities, sorcery and idols, everything his people trusted in his place, and judges the nations that will not listen (vv. 10–15).

Where it leads. To Christ by direct promise, the plainest in the book. When Herod asked where the Christ was to be born, the chief priests answered from verse 2 (Matthew 2:5–6), and Jesus was born in Bethlehem of David’s line: the eternal Son, who “was in the beginning with God” (John 1:2), entering the town of his ancestor. He is the shepherd who stands in the strength of the LORD and lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11), and “he himself is our peace” (Ephesians 2:14). Even the struck judge of verse 1 finds its echo in him: “they spit in his face and struck him” (Matthew 26:67). Our King came to his throne through humiliation.

For us. Our security is a person, not a system. Ask which horses and fortune-tellers you rely on, and let the King from Bethlehem take their place. And when your circumstances look as small and besieged as Micah’s Judah, remember where God began his greatest work: in a village too little to count.
5.theology:
God's chosen ruler comes from an overlooked village, and his origin is from ancient days (v. 2; John 1:1; Col 1:17; Matt 2:5-6).

God's promises often involve long waiting, measured out until the appointed birth (v. 3; Isa 7:14).

Christ is the shepherd-king who feeds the flock in God's strength, in contrast to leaders who devour it (v. 4; 3:1-3; John 10:11).

Peace is not an arrangement but a person: he himself is our peace (v. 5; Eph 2:14).

God is never short of deliverers for his people (vv. 5-6).

God's people among the nations are both a life-giving dew and, to those who resist God, a lion (vv. 7-8).

God graciously destroys the false securities of his own people, military, occult and idolatrous, so that they are left trusting him alone (vv. 10-14).
5.examples:
Israel's king is slapped on the cheek with a stick, and God's answer is a village too small to be listed, chosen to produce the ruler. The chief priests quoted the right verse and stayed where they were; knowing the Bible is not the same as going to Christ.

The shepherd from Bethlehem feeds the flock instead of eating it, and God is never short of deliverers. God's people are like dew that nobody ordered, appearing overnight on dry grass. And God takes away the chariots his people trusted, because what he removes is what would have failed them.

keyVerse.quote: But you, O Bethlehem Ephrathah, who are too little to be among the clans of Judah, from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel, whose coming forth is from of old, from ancient days.
keyVerse.note: This is the promise the whole chapter turns on, and the plainest prophecy of Christ in Micah. A humiliated king (v. 1) is answered by a ruler from the smallest of places whose origins reach back before Bethlehem itself. Seven centuries later the chief priests pointed Herod to this verse (Matthew 2:5–6), and the child was already there.

5.reflection:
God answers a besieged city and a humiliated king with a promise about a small village (vv. 1–2). Why do you think God so often begins his work in places and people the world overlooks? Where might he be doing that around you?

The chief priests knew verse 2 well enough to quote it, yet stayed in Jerusalem while the foreigners went to Bethlehem (Matthew 2:4–10). What is the difference between knowing about Christ and coming to him? Where are you tempted to settle for the first?

Micah says the King “shall be their peace” (v. 5), not only that he will bring it. What difference does it make that our peace is a person rather than a set of circumstances?

In verses 10–14 God removes horses, strongholds, fortune-tellers and idols. What are the modern equivalents you are tempted to trust for security or control, and how might God be loosening your grip on them?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The LORD Has an Indictment
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s case against his people rests on his kindness, and his demand rests on his grace. He summons the mountains and the foundations of the earth as witnesses (vv. 1–2), then asks how he has wearied his people and answers with what he did for them: the exodus, the leaders he gave, Balaam’s curse turned to blessing, and the crossing from Shittim to Gilgal (vv. 3–5). A worshipper, unsettled, offers more and more, from calves to rivers of oil to his own firstborn (vv. 6–7). The answer is not a higher price but what God has already said: do justice, love kindness and walk humbly with your God (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: God's complaint against his people is not that he has failed them but that they have forgotten his goodness, and what he wants is not a bigger offering but a changed life.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear what the LORD says: Arise, plead your case before the mountains, and let the hills hear your voice. Hear, you mountains, the indictment of the LORD, and you enduring foundations of the earth, for the LORD has an indictment against his people, and he will contend with Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God brings a lawsuit against his own people, with the ancient mountains as witnesses, because he will not let them go.

Plead your case before the mountains. The chapter opens as a courtroom, and the jury is the landscape. The “mountains” and the “enduring foundations of the earth” are summoned because they have been there from the beginning and have watched the whole history between God and his people. When the covenant was made, Moses called heaven and earth to witness (Deuteronomy 30:19); now they hear whether it has been kept.

He will contend with Israel. An “indictment” is a legal case. But there is tenderness in it: God will contend with Israel, his own people. He is not walking away from them; he is arguing with them, which is what you do with someone you refuse to lose.

verseByVerse.quote: "O my people, what have I done to you? How have I wearied you? Answer me! For I brought you up from the land of Egypt and redeemed you from the house of slavery, and I sent before you Moses, Aaron, and Miriam. O my people, remember what Balak king of Moab devised, and what Balaam the son of Beor answered him, and what happened from Shittim to Gilgal, that you may know the righteous acts of the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s case against his people is a list of his kindnesses: he has never wearied them, but redeemed them, led them, protected them and brought them home. Grace comes before any demand.

O my people, what have I done to you? God opens his case with a question that must have stunned them: not “How dare you?” but “what have I done to you?” The Judge of all the earth invites his people to state their complaint against him: have I asked too much?

I brought you up from the land of Egypt. His evidence is not a list of their failures but of his kindnesses. He “redeemed you from the house of slavery”: redemption means buying someone out of bondage, and they were slaves whom he set free at a price. Nor did he leave them leaderless: he gave them Moses, Aaron, and Miriam.

What Balak king of Moab devised. God recalls a rescue they never even saw. Balak hired the prophet Balaam to curse Israel, and God turned every curse into a blessing while Israel camped in the valley, unaware (Numbers 22–24). Then “from Shittim to Gilgal”: from their last camp east of the Jordan, where they had fallen into idolatry with Moab (Numbers 25:1–3), to their first camp in the promised land (Joshua 4:19). Even after Shittim, God brought them across the river.

The righteous acts of the LORD. These are the things he has done right by them, and this is the order of the Bible: grace first, then obedience. Before God asks anything of his people in verse 8, he reminds them of everything he has done for them in verses 4–5. Christians read the same order in the gospel: Christ has redeemed us, therefore we live for him.

From the cross. For many centuries the church has sung God’s question, “O my people, what have I done to you?”, on Good Friday, as if from the lips of the crucified Christ. It fits. He healed, fed, taught and forgave, and the answer to his question was a cross.

Why people drift. If we are honest, the answer to God’s question is usually that he has done nothing wrong at all. We simply wanted something else.
verseByVerse.note: Shittim to Gilgal was Israel’s crossing of the Jordan.

verseByVerse.quote: "With what shall I come before the LORD, and bow myself before God on high? Shall I come before him with burnt offerings, with calves a year old? Will the LORD be pleased with thousands of rams, with ten thousands of rivers of oil? Shall I give my firstborn for my transgression, the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Religion that thinks God must be bought keeps raising its price, even to a child, because it has never grasped that God gives before he asks.

With what shall I come before the LORD? Now a worshipper answers, and you can hear the panic rising. What will it take? He starts where the law starts, with “burnt offerings” and “calves a year old”, and then the offers grow wilder: “thousands of rams”, “ten thousands of rivers of oil” (the ESV notes the question may read “Will the LORD accept”). He keeps raising his own offer, like a man bidding against himself at an auction.

Shall I give my firstborn for my transgression? That was not merely rhetorical. King Ahaz, in Micah’s own lifetime, “burned his son as an offering” (2 Kings 16:3). This is where religion goes when it believes God must be bought: in the end it will pay anything, even a child.

The Bible’s final answer. Behind the escalation is an assumption still with us: that God is angry and can be bought off if the price is high enough, with money, with service, with self-punishment. The Bible’s final answer to “With what shall I come before the LORD?” is not verse 8 but the cross. God did give a firstborn son for transgression, and it was his own.

verseByVerse.quote: He has told you, O man, what is good; and what does the LORD require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God?
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has already shown his redeemed people what is good: not costly offerings, but justice in their dealings, a love of kindness, and a humble walk with him. It is the shape of a rescued life, not the price of rescue.

He has told you, O man, what is good. The verse everyone knows answers the panic of verses 6–7 with calm: God has already said what he wants, in the law and the prophets, and it was never rivers of oil.

To do justice. Not to admire it but to do it: pay fair wages, tell the truth in court, leave the poor man his field.

To love kindness. (The ESV notes this may be rendered “steadfast love”, the great covenant word for God’s loyal love; older translations such as the King James Version have “love mercy”.) Not merely to practise kindness but to love it: God wants people who delight in mercy, as he does (7:18), not people who ration it.

To walk humbly with your God. Here is the root of the other two. “Walk” is a whole life, step after step; “humbly” is the opposite of the proud plotters of chapter 2; and “with your God” is companionship, not servitude. Humility is not low self-esteem or a show of running yourself down. The worshipper of verses 6–7, for all his grovelling, is proud, because he still thinks he can name the price and pay it. Pride is the wish to stand before God on our own terms, owing him nothing, and it can wear sackcloth as easily as silk. To walk humbly is to stop bidding and go along with God: letting him lead, taking his word over our own, receiving instead of buying. In practice it often looks like a plain “I was wrong” where you would normally explain yourself. See also Humility in the Theological Dictionary.

The one who stooped. The one who truly walked humbly was God’s own Son. Though he was in the form of God, “he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross” (Philippians 2:8), and he still invites the weary to walk with him: “for I am gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29). It is hard to strut beside someone who stooped that low for you.

Christ kept it for us. Only Christ has kept this verse perfectly, and he kept it in our place, so that his obedience is counted as ours. By his Spirit everyone who belongs to him is being remade into the kind of person it describes.

How do I love kindness? Loved kindness shows in small, repeated choices. Go first. Do not wait to be asked: the meal for the family with a new baby, the message to the friend who has gone quiet. Give more than is owed. Justice pays the bill; kindness lets the small debt go and gives the second chance. Keep it up when it is not returned. Covenant love is loyal love: it keeps visiting the difficult relative and keeps praying for the neighbour who never says thank you. Let it start at home. The tone you use with your own family at the end of a long day is where kindness is tested most. All of this is a reflection, not an achievement: “Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 4:32). We learn to love kindness by receiving it: “when the goodness and loving kindness of God our Savior appeared, he saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy” (Titus 3:4–5).

Two easy mistakes. The first is to treat this verse as a ladder: do these three things and you will be acceptable. But God has already redeemed these people from slavery (vv. 4–5); and we are “justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” (Romans 3:24), for none of us has done justice, loved kindness and walked humbly as we should. The second is to talk about grace and ignore what this verse requires. Jesus would not allow that: he rebuked religious experts who tithed their garden herbs and neglected “the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faithfulness” (Matthew 23:23). Hold both.

Isn’t this verse all the religion anyone needs? It is quoted in speeches and printed on posters as faith reduced to its essentials: be fair, be kind, be humble, and leave doctrine to others. But read the verse slowly and try living it: justice in every deal and every conversation; kindness loved, not merely shown when convenient; a humble walk with God, owning that he has the first claim on your whole life. Anyone who takes it seriously for a week finds that it does not lower the bar but lifts it out of reach, and we are back with the worshipper of verses 6–7, asking what we can bring. The person who says, “I just try to live by Micah 6:8,” has chosen exactly the right verse. Read honestly, it will bring him to the end of himself, and to the God who has already answered the question of verse 6 at the cross.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–16 — Wicked Scales and Empty Harvests
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will not overlook dishonesty in the marketplace, and a people built on cheating will find their gains turn to nothing. The LORD’s voice calls to the city, and fearing his name is wisdom (v. 9). He has seen the treasures gained by wickedness: short measures, false scales and bags of light weights, the violence of the rich and the lies of everyone else (vv. 10–12). So he will strike them with futility: they will eat and stay hungry, sow and not reap, press olives and grapes and never enjoy them (vv. 13–15). Judah has followed the statutes of Omri and Ahab, and will share their scorn (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: Dishonest gain is never blessed, and a people who copy the worst of their history inherit its ruin.

verseByVerse.quote: The voice of the LORD cries to the city— and it is sound wisdom to fear your name: "Hear of the rod and of him who appointed it! Can I forget any longer the treasures of wickedness in the house of the wicked, and the scant measure that is accursed? Shall I acquit the man with wicked scales and with a bag of deceitful weights? Your rich men are full of violence; your inhabitants speak lies, and their tongue is deceitful in their mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God hears the dishonesty of the marketplace, the short measure and the rigged scales, and he will not acquit those who grow rich by cheating, violence and lies.

The voice of the LORD cries to the city. God’s voice calls to the city, and Micah breaks in to say that “it is sound wisdom to fear your name”. Fearing God is not superstition; it is realism, and the wisest thing a city can do.

A bag of deceitful weights. What God has been watching is startlingly small-scale: “the scant measure”, “wicked scales”, “a bag of deceitful weights”. A merchant carried stone weights in a bag; a dishonest one carried two sets, a heavy stone for buying and a light one for selling. God’s law said, “You shall have just balances, just weights” (Leviticus 19:36).

Shall I acquit the man with wicked scales? God notices the shop counter: not only wars and injustice in high places, but the short weight, the padded invoice, the hours claimed and not worked. The question expects the answer no.

Your rich men are full of violence. Verse 12 moves from the scales to the tongue: the rich are “full of violence”, and the ordinary people “speak lies”. Cheating in business and lying in speech are the same disease showing itself in different places.

Honest scales and the gospel. When Jesus came to the house of Zacchaeus, the tax collector did not wait to be told what to do: “if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold” (Luke 19:8). Grace that reaches a man reaches his accounts.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that the meaning of the Hebrew in the last part of verse 9 is uncertain; the sense seems to be a call to heed the rod of judgment and to recognise who has appointed it. In verse 10 the ESV notes an alternative reading, “Are there still treasures”. Either way, God has not forgotten wealth gained by wickedness.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I strike you with a grievous blow, making you desolate because of your sins. You shall eat, but not be satisfied, and there shall be hunger within you; you shall put away, but not preserve, and what you preserve I will give to the sword. You shall sow, but not reap; you shall tread olives, but not anoint yourselves with oil; you shall tread grapes, but not drink wine. For you have kept the statutes of Omri, and all the works of the house of Ahab; and you have walked in their counsels, that I may make you a desolation, and your inhabitants a hissing; so you shall bear the scorn of my people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because Judah has copied the worst kings of Israel, God will make its labour futile: food that does not satisfy, savings that do not last, harvests others enjoy.

You shall eat, but not be satisfied. The judgment is futility. They will eat without being satisfied, store food they will not keep, sow fields that others will reap, and tread olives and grapes for oil and wine they will never enjoy. This is exactly what God’s covenant had warned centuries earlier (Deuteronomy 28:38–40).

The statutes of Omri. The last verse names the pattern they have copied. Omri founded a royal dynasty in the northern kingdom and “did what was evil in the sight of the LORD” (1 Kings 16:25), and his son Ahab, with Jezebel, made Baal worship the state religion and murdered Naboth for his vineyard. Judah had watched all that, seen the north destroyed for it, and adopted the same policies. (The ESV notes the Hebrew of this verse reads, “For the statutes of Omri are kept”.)

Gain without blessing. Gain that God does not bless does not satisfy. People can accumulate for years and find at the end that they are still hungry. Jesus offers what the futile harvest never could: “whoever comes to me shall not hunger” (John 6:35).

Copying the worst. Nations, churches and families copy the worst of their own history with remarkable persistence, and it ends in “scorn”. Yet the God who brings this indictment is the same God who, one chapter later, delights in steadfast love and casts sins into the depths of the sea. The way back from the false scales is not a better record but confession to him.

6.title: What Does the LORD Require of You?
6.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 6 opens the third and last round of the book (chapters 6 and 7), again with the call “Hear” (v. 1). After the bright promises of chapters 4 and 5, Micah brings us back to the present: God has a case against his people.

The message. God takes his people to court, but his evidence is his own kindness, and his question is “what have I done to you?” (v. 3). He does not want a religion that tries to buy him with ever larger offerings; he has already redeemed his people and told them what is good: to do justice, to love kindness and to walk humbly with him (v. 8). Because they have done the opposite, cheating at the scales and copying the worst kings of Israel, their labour will come to nothing.

Why it was said. Judah was full of religious activity and commercial dishonesty at the same time (see the introduction). People sacrificed generously, King Ahaz even his own son, while merchants used false weights; they had forgotten what God had done for them and imagined he could be paid.

How the chapter makes its case. With the mountains as witnesses (vv. 1–2), God states his case, a list of his kindnesses: the exodus, Moses, Aaron and Miriam, Balaam’s curse turned to blessing, the crossing into the land (vv. 3–5). A worshipper asks what will satisfy God and raises his bid to his own firstborn (vv. 6–7), and is answered: God has already told you what is good (v. 8). Then God turns to the city. False measures, violence and lies (vv. 9–12) will bring a judgment of futility, eating without being satisfied and sowing without reaping (vv. 13–15), because Judah has kept the statutes of Omri and Ahab (v. 16).

Where it leads. To Christ by the need it exposes and by the character of God it reveals. The worshipper’s question, “With what shall I come before the LORD?” (v. 6), has no answer he can pay. God answered it himself: he did not spare his own Son, but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32). And verse 8, which none of us has kept, was kept perfectly by Jesus, who did justice, loved mercy and walked in humble obedience to his Father “to the point of death, even death on a cross” (Philippians 2:8).

For us. We are tempted either to bargain with God or to talk about grace and ignore justice. This chapter closes both doors: grace comes first, and grace produces honest scales, kind hearts and a humble walk. Let what God has done for you in Christ be the place where your obedience starts.
6.theology:
God argues with his people rather than abandoning them, and calls creation to witness (vv. 1-2).

God's case against us rests on his kindness, not our excuses; grace comes before demand (vv. 3-5).

Religion that tries to buy God will pay any price and never find peace; only God’s own gift answers the question, “With what shall I come before the LORD?” (vv. 6-7; Rom 3:24-25).

What God requires is justice done, mercy loved and a humble walk with him: the shape of a redeemed life, not the price of redemption (v. 8; Deut 10:12; Matt 23:23).

God watches the shop counter: short measures and false weights are sins he will not acquit (vv. 10-11; Lev 19:36; Prov 11:1).

Gain God does not bless does not satisfy; futility is itself a judgment (vv. 14-15; Deut 28:38-40).

Copying the worst patterns of our history leads to the same ruin those patterns produced (v. 16; 1 Kgs 16:25-33).
6.examples:
The chapter works through pictures that stay in the mind. The mountains sit as a jury, and the Judge asks his own people what he has done wrong. A frightened worshipper bids against himself, from calves to rivers of oil to his own child, and is answered by three plain requirements.

Then the scene shrinks to a merchant's bag with two sets of weights in it, and to men pressing olives for oil they will never use, because a southern kingdom chose to copy the policies that had destroyed the north.

keyVerse.quote: He has told you, O man, what is good; and what does the LORD require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God?
keyVerse.note: The most quoted verse in Micah answers the worshipper’s anxious bidding (vv. 6–7) with what God has always wanted. Coming straight after God’s list of his saving acts (vv. 4–5), it describes how the redeemed live, not the price of redemption. Read honestly, its demands also drive us to Christ, the only one who has fully kept it.

6.reflection:
God answers the charge against his people by asking, “O my people, what have I done to you?” (v. 3), and then lists his kindnesses. When you drift from God, what is usually the real reason? How does remembering what he has done for you in Christ draw you back?

The worshipper of verses 6–7 keeps raising his offer, even to his firstborn. In what ways do people today, Christians included, still try to pay God off with effort, giving or self-punishment? How does the cross answer his question?

Take the three parts of verse 8 in turn. Where in your work, your home and your church is God calling you to do justice, to love kindness rather than ration it, and to walk humbly with him?

God notices short measures and “a bag of deceitful weights” (vv. 10–11). What are their equivalents in our economy and in your own working life, and what might honesty cost you this week?
