verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — No One Upright Is Left
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When a society is rotten all the way through, the believer’s hope is to look to the LORD. Micah is like a hungry man in an orchard after the harvest: he longs for one ripe fig, one upright person, and finds none, only people hunting each other like game (vv. 1–2). Prince, judge and great man weave their corruption together, and even the best of them are thorns (vv. 3–4). Trust collapses inward until a man’s enemies are the men of his own house (vv. 5–6). Then comes the turn: “But as for me, I will look to the LORD”, waiting for the God who will hear (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: When society and even family fail, the believer's answer is not despair but waiting on God.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe is me! For I have become as when the summer fruit has been gathered, as when the grapes have been gleaned: there is no cluster to eat, no first-ripe fig that my soul desires. The godly has perished from the earth, and there is no one upright among mankind; they all lie in wait for blood, and each hunts the other with a net. Their hands are on what is evil, to do it well; the prince and the judge ask for a bribe, and the great man utters the evil desire of his soul; thus they weave it together. The best of them is like a brier, the most upright of them a thorn hedge. The day of your watchmen, of your punishment, has come; now their confusion is at hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Micah grieves that no faithful person is left: everyone preys on everyone else, the powerful conspire, and the day of punishment has come.

Woe is me! Micah is a hungry man in an orchard after the pickers have been through, longing for a “first-ripe fig”, the early fig that is the best of the season, and finding “no cluster to eat”.

The godly has perished from the earth. The missing fruit is godly people. The Hebrew word for “the godly” is related to the word for steadfast love (6:8; 7:18): it means people who are loyal, kind and faithful. Instead “each hunts the other with a net”, as if people were game.

Their hands are on what is evil. Corruption has become a craft: their hands are on evil “to do it well”. Prince, judge and great man “weave it together”, as strands are twisted into one rope. Corruption is rarely one person; it is a network, and each strand makes the others stronger.

The best of them is like a brier. Even the best of them scratches and tears. And “the day of your watchmen” has come: the day of punishment that the prophets, Israel’s watchmen, warned about.

Not statistics but grief. Micah is not giving statistics; he is a grieving man who looked for one honest person and found none, as anyone who has watched a workplace or a church go bad will understand. Paul gathers laments like this to show that “None is righteous, no, not one” (Romans 3:10), and God’s answer was not to find one upright man but to send one: his Son, the Righteous One.

Uncertain wording. The verb translated “weave it together” is rare in Hebrew, and its exact sense is uncertain; most take it of twisting strands together. That they conspire is clear.

verseByVerse.quote: Put no trust in a neighbor; have no confidence in a friend; guard the doors of your mouth from her who lies in your arms; for the son treats the father with contempt, the daughter rises up against her mother, the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; a man's enemies are the men of his own house. But as for me, I will look to the LORD; I will wait for the God of my salvation; my God will hear me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When betrayal reaches even the home, Micah turns to the LORD, waits for him, and is sure that God will hear.

Put no trust in a neighbor. When a society rots, it rots inward, until it reaches the last place people expect: home. Do not confide in a neighbour, or a friend, or even the wife who “lies in your arms” (the ESV notes the Hebrew word is “bosom”). Children despise parents; in-laws turn on each other. “A man’s enemies are the men of his own house.”

As Jesus used it. Jesus quoted these words in a new setting: his coming would divide households, so that “a person’s enemies will be those of his own household” (Matthew 10:35–36), because some in a family follow him and others refuse. Micah describes a family breaking apart through sin; Jesus warns that a family may break apart over him. Many Christians know the second first-hand. He does not promise that our households will be united; he promises that he is worth the cost.

But as for me, I will look to the LORD. Verse 7 is the hinge of the chapter and a great verse for dark times. Three things hold Micah steady. “I will look to the LORD”: a deliberate act of attention, away from the mess and toward God. “I will wait for the God of my salvation”: he does not expect an instant answer, and he does not stop expecting one. “My God will hear me”: not “may hear”, but “will”.

Honest lament first. This comes after, not instead of, honest lament. The Bible never asks us to pretend things are fine. It asks us to look up while telling the truth about what is down here.

How do I wait for the LORD? Waiting is not doing nothing; it is where you put your weight while nothing seems to change. Look away on purpose. When the news or the 2 a.m. worry fills your mind, turn to God in a sentence of prayer. Hold on to a promise. Take one word of God into the waiting and keep returning to it: “I wait for the LORD, my soul waits, and in his word I hope” (Psalm 130:5). Keep doing the next right thing. Micah went on telling the truth in a city that did not want it; waiting is faithfulness in the meantime, not giving up. Say “will”, not “may”. Tell God, and yourself, that he will hear. The ground for that confidence is the cross: “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32). The God of our salvation has already given the greatest gift, so we can wait for the rest.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — When I Fall, I Shall Rise
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s people may fall under his discipline, but they will rise, because the God who judges them will also plead their cause. Zion tells her gloating enemy that her fall is not final: the LORD will be her light in the darkness (v. 8). She bears his anger because she has sinned, and waits for him to vindicate her and to shame the enemy who mocked, “Where is the LORD your God?” (vv. 9–10). Then a day of rebuilding is announced: the walls rise, the boundary is extended, and people stream in from Assyria and Egypt, while the earth reaps the fruit of its deeds (vv. 11–13).
verseByVerse.theology: A believer who has fallen under God's hand can still be sure of rising, because the God who disciplines is the God who vindicates.

verseByVerse.quote: Rejoice not over me, O my enemy; when I fall, I shall rise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD will be a light to me. I will bear the indignation of the LORD because I have sinned against him, until he pleads my cause and executes judgment for me. He will bring me out to the light; I shall look upon his vindication. Then my enemy will see, and shame will cover her who said to me, "Where is the LORD your God?" My eyes will look upon her; now she will be trampled down like the mire of the streets.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s fallen people accept his discipline for their sin, yet tell their enemy not to gloat, because the LORD will plead their cause and bring them into the light.

When I fall, I shall rise. Now God’s people speak, beaten and mocked. Not “if” but “when”: she knows she will fall, and she knows she will not stay down, because rising is not something she does for herself: “the LORD will be a light to me”. Proverbs says the same: “the righteous falls seven times and rises again” (Proverbs 24:16). The difference between a believer and an unbeliever is not that one falls and the other does not, but what happens next.

Because I have sinned against him. A remarkably mature confession: she does not protest her innocence, she accepts the discipline, and she is certain it will end, “until he pleads my cause”.

Judge and advocate. God is the judge who has sentenced her, and also the advocate who will plead her case. That seems impossible until the cross. Paul asks, “Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies”, and answers that Christ Jesus “is at the right hand of God, who indeed is interceding for us” (Romans 8:33–34).

Where is the LORD your God? The oldest jeer in the world (compare Psalm 42:10), and it stings because at the time there is no visible answer. It was flung at Jesus on the cross: “He trusts in God; let God deliver him now” (Matthew 27:43). The answer came on the third day. It comes later, and from God, not from us.

verseByVerse.quote: A day for the building of your walls! In that day the boundary shall be far extended. In that day they will come to you, from Assyria and the cities of Egypt, and from Egypt to the River, from sea to sea and from mountain to mountain. But the earth will be desolate because of its inhabitants, for the fruit of their deeds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ruined Zion will be rebuilt and enlarged, and people will stream to her even from her old enemies, while the earth reaps what it has sown.

A day for the building of your walls! After the darkness, a shout. The ruined city of 3:12 will be rebuilt, and its boundary pushed far out.

From Assyria and the cities of Egypt. People will come from Assyria and Egypt, the superpowers that had terrorised Israel, and from as far as “the River” (the ESV notes this means the Euphrates). The old enemies are now pilgrims, arriving from every direction (the ESV notes that the Hebrew reads “he” where the ESV has “they”). This is the vision of chapter 4: the nations streaming to God’s mountain.

Walls pushed out. In Christ the walls take in the nations: Gentiles who come to him are “no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God” (Ephesians 2:19).

The earth will be desolate. Alongside the ingathering stands the sober fact of judgment. The world reaps “the fruit of their deeds”, and out of that world God gathers a people from every nation.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “boundary” in verse 11 can also mean “decree”, and the phrase “be far” can mean “far extended” or “far removed”, so some older translations speak of a decree (perhaps of oppressors) being far removed. The ESV’s reading, a city whose borders grow, fits the walls and the crowds of verse 12.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–20 — Who Is a God Like You?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The book ends with a prayer, a promise and a song of wonder at a God who pardons. Micah asks the LORD to shepherd his flock with his own staff and give them back the rich pastures of old (v. 14). God answers that he will show them marvellous things as at the exodus, and the proud nations will come trembling out of their strongholds and turn in fear to him (vv. 15–17). Then Micah’s own name becomes a question of praise: who is a God like you, who pardons, will not keep his anger, delights in steadfast love, treads down our iniquities, casts our sins into the sea and keeps his oath to Jacob and Abraham (vv. 18–20)?
verseByVerse.theology: The last word of Micah is not judgment but a God whose willingness to forgive has no equal.

verseByVerse.quote: Shepherd your people with your staff, the flock of your inheritance, who dwell alone in a forest in the midst of a garden land; let them graze in Bashan and Gilead as in the days of old. As in the days when you came out of the land of Egypt, I will show them marvelous things. The nations shall see and be ashamed of all their might; they shall lay their hands on their mouths; their ears shall be deaf; they shall lick the dust like a serpent, like the crawling things of the earth; they shall come trembling out of their strongholds; they shall turn in dread to the LORD our God, and they shall be in fear of you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Micah prays for God himself to shepherd his flock, and God promises wonders like the exodus that will bring the proud nations trembling to him.

Shepherd your people with your staff. After the corrupt shepherds of chapter 3, Micah asks the true Shepherd to take the work himself. The prayer is answered in the King of 5:4, who will “shepherd his flock in the strength of the LORD”, and in Jesus, the good shepherd (John 10:11).

Who dwell alone in a forest. The flock is isolated in scrub amid “a garden land” (the ESV notes the Hebrew says “of Carmel”, the fertile ridge), so Micah asks for grazing in Bashan and Gilead again, the best pasture Israel had held and among the first lands it lost, when the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser took Gilead in Micah’s own day (2 Kings 15:29), so the prayer asks God to give back what judgment had taken.

I will show them marvelous things. God answers, and his answer reaches back to the exodus: “As in the days when you came out of the land of Egypt” (the ESV notes the Hebrew reads “him”). He has not changed, and may be asked to act again.

The nations shall see and be ashamed. The proud nations end with hands over their mouths. They “lick the dust like a serpent”, sharing the humiliation of the serpent of Eden (Genesis 3:14), and come “trembling out of their strongholds”, the fortresses they trusted. Yet the last phrase turns even this toward hope: “they shall turn in dread to the LORD our God”. They turn to him. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 9:10), and for some it is the beginning of salvation.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is a God like you, pardoning iniquity and passing over transgression for the remnant of his inheritance? He does not retain his anger forever, because he delights in steadfast love. He will again have compassion on us; he will tread our iniquities underfoot. You will cast all our sins into the depths of the sea. You will show faithfulness to Jacob and steadfast love to Abraham, as you have sworn to our fathers from the days of old.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No god is like the LORD, because he delights to pardon and keeps his sworn promise to Abraham’s children; the cross shows how he does it and stays just.

Who is a God like you? The book ends in wonder. After all the charges (stolen fields, bought verdicts, false weights), Micah asks the question of his own name, and the answer is nobody: not because of God’s power but because of his pardon.

He delights in steadfast love. Look at the words. “Pardoning iniquity”: lifting the guilt off. “Passing over transgression”: stepping past what he could have stopped to punish. “He does not retain his anger forever”: he will not nurse a grievance, though he has the best of reasons. And then the reason for all of it: “because he delights in steadfast love”. God does not forgive reluctantly. Mercy is what he enjoys. Micah echoes the name God proclaimed to Moses (Exodus 34:6–7).

Two pictures of forgiveness. Both repay a slow reading. God will “tread our iniquities underfoot”, crushing them like an enemy. And he “will cast all our sins into the depths of the sea” (the ESV notes the Hebrew reads “their”). Not into the shallows, where they can be fished out, but into the depths, where nothing is recovered. As Pharaoh’s chariots were cast into the sea (Exodus 15:4), our sins go down, never to pursue us again.

How can a just God pass over transgression? Micah could not fully answer this; the New Testament does. God “put forward” Christ “as a propitiation by his blood”, that is, a sacrifice that turns away God’s just anger, precisely to show his righteousness while passing over sins (Romans 3:25). Micah’s wonder is right, and the cross is where it is explained.

As you have sworn to our fathers. The last verse grounds all this mercy in something outside us: the promise God has sworn to our fathers, to Jacob and Abraham, centuries before. Our forgiveness does not rest on our performance but on God’s oath.

Where the gospel begins. When Zechariah held his newborn son and prophesied about the coming of Christ, he said God had acted “to show the mercy promised to our fathers and to remember his holy covenant, the oath that he swore to our father Abraham” (Luke 1:72–73). Micah ends where the gospel begins: an unbreakable promise, a God who delights in mercy, and sins thrown into the sea.

Where God has put them. He removes our transgressions “as far as the east is from the west” (Psalm 103:12), and promises in the new covenant, “I will remember their sins no more” (Hebrews 8:12). Christians who keep dragging their forgiven sins back up to the surface should notice where God has put them.
verseByVerse.note: Micah’s name means “Who is like the LORD?”, the question echoed in v. 18.

7.title: Who Is a God Like You?
7.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 7 closes the third round of Micah’s preaching and the whole book. After God’s case against a cheating city in chapter 6, the prophet speaks for himself, then for his fallen people, and the book ends in prayer and praise.

The message. When everything around you is rotten and no one can be trusted, look to the LORD and wait for him. His people may fall under his discipline because they have sinned, but he will plead their cause, bring them into the light, rebuild and shepherd them. Above all he is a God like no other: holy enough to judge, yet delighting to pardon, treading down our iniquities and casting all our sins into the depths of the sea, because he keeps his oath to Abraham.

Why it was said. Micah’s Judah was a society where judges took bribes and families turned on one another, with invasion and exile ahead (see the introduction). The faithful few needed to know how to live there, and whether God’s promises could survive his people’s sin.

How the chapter makes its case. Micah laments like a hungry man in a stripped orchard: no one upright is left, rulers weave corruption together, and even the home is unsafe (vv. 1–6). But as for him, he will look to the LORD (v. 7). Then Zion answers her gloating enemy: she has fallen and bears God’s anger for her sin, but he will plead her cause and she will rise (vv. 8–10). A day of rebuilding and ingathering is promised, while the earth reaps its deeds (vv. 11–13). Micah prays for the flock, God promises marvels as at the exodus, and the nations come trembling (vv. 14–17). The book ends with Micah’s own name turned into praise: “Who is a God like you?” (vv. 18–20).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise and by the character of God revealed in him. The God who “delights in steadfast love” can pass over transgression and remain just only because he put forward his Son “as a propitiation by his blood” (Romans 3:25); the cross is where our sins are trodden down and drowned. The Judge who becomes his people’s advocate (v. 9) is seen in Christ, who is at God’s right hand interceding for us (Romans 8:34). And when Zechariah greeted the coming of Christ, he sang of “the oath that he swore to our father Abraham” (Luke 1:73), the oath on which Micah ends.

For us. Micah shows how to live in a dark time: tell the truth about it, look up, wait, and keep going. And he shows where to take our guilt: not into endless self-reproach, but to the God who has cast it into the depths of the sea. Leave it there.
7.theology:
A society can decay until honesty is hard to find and corruption becomes a skilled, cooperative craft (vv. 2-4).

Sin finally reaches the family, and the gospel too can divide households, though for a very different reason (vv. 5-6; Matt 10:35-36).

The believer's response to a collapsing world is to look to the LORD, wait for him and expect to be heard (v. 7).

God's people fall, but they rise, because their rising depends on God's light rather than their strength (v. 8; Prov 24:16).

A believer may accept God's discipline as deserved and still be certain of vindication, for the Judge is also the advocate (v. 9; Rom 8:33-34).

God gathers the old enemies as pilgrims, even while the world reaps the fruit of its deeds (vv. 12-13; 4:1-2).

God forgives not reluctantly but gladly, because he delights in steadfast love (v. 18; Rom 3:25).

Forgiven sins are removed beyond recovery, and our security rests on God's sworn promise, fulfilled in Christ (vv. 19-20; Ps 103:12; Heb 8:12; Luke 1:72-73).
7.examples:
The chapter moves from a hungry man in a stripped orchard, and officials twisting their schemes together like strands of rope, to a household where no one can safely speak.

Then the light breaks in: a believer who says “when I fall”, not “if”; a Judge who sentences and then pleads the prisoner's case; old enemies arriving as pilgrims; and sins thrown into water too deep for anyone to fish them out again.

keyVerse.quote: Who is a God like you, pardoning iniquity and passing over transgression for the remnant of his inheritance? He does not retain his anger forever, because he delights in steadfast love.
keyVerse.note: The book closes with the question hidden in Micah’s own name, and answers it with God’s pardon rather than his power. After seven chapters of charges, the last word is that the LORD delights in steadfast love, a mercy the cross shows to be both free and just (Romans 3:25–26).

7.reflection:
Micah looks for one upright person and finds none, yet says, “But as for me, I will look to the LORD” (v. 7). When you are discouraged by the state of your workplace, church or country, what does looking to the LORD and waiting for him look like in practice?

In verse 9 God’s people say, “I will bear the indignation of the LORD because I have sinned against him,” and yet expect him to plead their cause. How does the cross make it possible for the Judge to be our advocate (Romans 8:33–34)?

Jesus applied verse 6 to the divisions his coming would bring to families (Matthew 10:35–36). Have you known the cost of following Christ in your own household? How can we pray for and support those who do?

Verses 18–19 say God delights in steadfast love and casts all our sins into the depths of the sea. Are there forgiven sins you keep dragging back up? What would it mean to leave them where God has put them?
